articles.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
articles.body:
I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.
A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than $1.8 billion in revenue the day it was released. 
Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy. 
But GTA 6 has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife. Previous GTA games were set in fictionalized versions of New York City and Hollywood, but the new one returns to Vice City, its version of Miami, which was also the setting for 2002’s installment. Unlike that game, however, GTA 6’s South Florida is complete with dozens of species of birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, mammals, and other creatures. The in-game Progress menu tracks all kinds of items to find, including 338 vehicles, 205 weapons, and, of primary interest to me, at least 60 bird species.
I made it my mission to find them all as quickly as possible.
(Side note: Pre-release marketing for GTA 6 touted 62 bird species, but the official birds Progress screen only lists 60, with a handful of others listed on the hunting screen.)
I am one hour in and I’ve found 16/60 birds https://t.co/81x42O1BuY
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
You begin the game as Jason, a low-level criminal working to raise money to support his young family. You’re equipped with zoom binoculars before the very first mission—tracking drug runners through a swamp and escaping with the seaplane—and I used them immediately, stopping mid-lurk to scan some Double-crested Cormorants on a dock. (Distracted from the job at hand to look at birds—just like real life!) They looked like Double-crested Cormorants!
After the first mission the player is free to explore the entirety of the map, stealing cars, robbing stores, or just birding wherever they want. The game makes birding easy: Looking at any bird through the in-game binoculars gives players the option to hold a button to “study” it, thereby adding it to the Progress menu. Simply standing on the back deck of Jason’s first safehouse yields a bunch of species like Brown Pelican and Laughing Gull. It’s just like being in South Florida!
Looking south from the back deck, I spotted another bird perched on an adjacent dock, with a few people gathered at the end. Looking through my binoculars I spotted my first Herring Gull—and noticed that the people, a woman and three men, were fully and visibly naked. Jason apparently lives next to a nudist resort. It’s just like being in South Florida!
Two down, 58 to go. I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets, before venturing out into the huge map. My strategy for finding birds in GTA 6 was the same as finding birds in real life: look in as many habitats as I could find. I started by “borrowing” a fanboat off a nearby dock and heading back to the swampy areas near the seaplane mission. There were tons of birds across the open water and in the marsh: Caspian Terns, Mottled Ducks, Sanderlings, Spotted Sandpipers, Great Blue Herons, Glossy and White Ibis, and … flocks of Whooping Cranes?
incredibly healthy populations of critically-endangered Whooping Cranes across Vice City. Huge if true. https://t.co/doe6oMOvBX
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
In fact, I found a number of avian inaccuracies in just my first few hours of playtime. Certain species like Whooping Crane and Red-cockaded Woodpecker are common throughout the map, despite being endangered and threatened, respectively, in real life. Golden Eagles are extremely rare in Florida, but I found one soaring over the Mt. Kalaga area (mountains, one may point out, aren’t found in Florida either). Some species have confusing naming quirks—the chickadee is Black-capped instead of Carolina, and there’s a “New World Oriole” instead of a Baltimore Oriole—but those changes are likely due to the fact that Carolina and Baltimore don’t exist in the GTA universe.
Though some of the inaccuracies may feel like a letdown in a game that is being hailed as the Greatest of All Time, I think it’s important to remember that it’s also game where you can get a ride from a dog driving a jet ski. Grand Theft Auto games are meant to be fun, not science. Plus, despite some of the misfires, the avifauna feels well thought-out. The map is true to the ecological boundaries of South Florida, with herons, gulls, and other waterbirds in the south while birds like Red-bellied Woodpecker, Wood Stork, and American Robin are found farther north. Birders know that certain exotic species have made their home in tropical South Florida, including Spot-breasted Oriole and Red Junglefowl, both in the game.
That geographic fidelity is the main tip for anyone looking to check off all the game’s birds: Find their habitat. The game doesn’t tell you what species to look for, so you’ll need to cover a lot of ground to find everything. Wading birds, shorebirds, and seabirds are common in the southern coastal part of the map. A number of smaller, open-country or forest birds are found up north. Owls come out at night. Birds in zoos and domestic farmyard birds count towards the 60, too, so don’t overlook those areas.
Wild Boar roadkill. It’s just like birding in Florida! https://t.co/gT84IticOK
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
The most accurate aspect is the actual landscape. Having birded extensively across South Florida myself, the habitats are immediately recognizable, from the pebbly mangrove beaches at the Keys to the grassy swamps further north. The setting feels absolutely real, from the fonts on the roadside fruit stands to the roadkill alongside the highways. (I found dead wild boar and dead deer by the side of the road, and a Turkey Vulture somehow flew into a building I was in and died at my feet.) 
So, if you’re up for the kind of funhouse-mirror version of Florida that the game presents, you can have a blast, and adding birdwatching into the insane free-for-all makes for some delightful moments. This guy just wanted to look at a gull but ended up chucking a woman off a pier. I’ve made myself laugh out loud by screeching to a halt in the middle of busy highways or intersections and jumping out of my car to look for birds while motorist behind me scream and swear. I love it.
easily my favorite thing to do so far is just screech to a halt in the middle of a busy intersection and start birding https://t.co/QsDOLmNfYq
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
As I was dodging dirt-biking rednecks to look for species in a northerly forest, I couldn’t help but compare birding in GTA 6 to birding in Red Dead Redemption 2 (RDR2), the latest installment in Rockstar’s other huge franchise. Birds and birding are presented quite similarly in both games, including the binocular “study” mechanic and many of the same species, but the experiences are totally different. RDR2 was set in the late 1800s, and players rode on horseback or locomotive through a comparatively wide-open and untrammeled version of America. There was mayhem in that game, too—outlaw gangs and marauders—but there were many peaceful moments, too, when a player could look out across wild landscape with nothing but nature as a soundtrack.
Not so in GTA 6. There’s plenty of birdsong on the soundtrack, but it competes with an endless racket of car radios, revving engines, swearing pedestrians, and blaring horns. There’s garbage almost everywhere, lapping the shorelines and blowing along the streets. There seems to be no inch of landscape in GTA 6 that hasn’t been lessened by the touch of humans. It is, I have to admit, a realistic depiction of birding in South Florida.
Birders working to fill out their GTA VI wildlife checklists should know something I just found out: THERE’S A ZOO https://t.co/2xN0joPKcR
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 20, 2026
Though GTA 6 provides what feels the most accurate version of modern birding ever put to screen, obsessing over the realism misses the point of having fun. Birders can, and should, visit the real South Florida to find the actual birds depicted in the game (and many more), but they can’t do it while also jumping over broken highway bridges on a stolen motorcycle. Birding is a bonus in GTA 6; mayhem is the draw.
I played for two hours after midnight, then about six straight hours Thursday before having to call it quits to write this column. In that time I found 50 of the 60 species listed in the “birds” compendium. I jumped back in this morning before work and found a huge chunk of species at a zoo (makes sense!) and on a farm, then found the 60th and final, an American Barn Owl, on a water tank in a town in the north of the map. Success! 
The biggest thing I can confirm is that all 60 birds on this list are available immediately, without needing any story progression. In Red Dead Redemption 2, some bird species were only found in Guarma, only accessible later in the game
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 20, 2026
I felt a wave of satisfaction, and while I’m not certain if I was the first one to find them all, when I posted about it, a Rockstar designer replied with, “History!” I’d met my goal, and celebrated in a way that only Grand Theft Auto games allow: by driving my car full speed off a cliff into the ocean.

articles.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
articles.body:
I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.
A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than $1.8 billion in revenue the day it was released. 
Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy. 
But GTA 6 has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife. Previous GTA games were set in fictionalized versions of New York City and Hollywood, but the new one returns to Vice City, its version of Miami, which was also the setting for 2002’s installment. Unlike that game, however, GTA 6’s South Florida is complete with dozens of species of birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, mammals, and other creatures. The in-game Progress menu tracks all kinds of items to find, including 338 vehicles, 205 weapons, and, of primary interest to me, at least 60 bird species.
I made it my mission to find them all as quickly as possible.
(Side note: Pre-release marketing for GTA 6 touted 62 bird species, but the official birds Progress screen only lists 60, with a handful of others listed on the hunting screen.)
I am one hour in and I’ve found 16/60 birds https://t.co/81x42O1BuY
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
You begin the game as Jason, a low-level criminal working to raise money to support his young family. You’re equipped with zoom binoculars before the very first mission—tracking drug runners through a swamp and escaping with the seaplane—and I used them immediately, stopping mid-lurk to scan some Double-crested Cormorants on a dock. (Distracted from the job at hand to look at birds—just like real life!) They looked like Double-crested Cormorants!
After the first mission the player is free to explore the entirety of the map, stealing cars, robbing stores, or just birding wherever they want. The game makes birding easy: Looking at any bird through the in-game binoculars gives players the option to hold a button to “study” it, thereby adding it to the Progress menu. Simply standing on the back deck of Jason’s first safehouse yields a bunch of species like Brown Pelican and Laughing Gull. It’s just like being in South Florida!
Looking south from the back deck, I spotted another bird perched on an adjacent dock, with a few people gathered at the end. Looking through my binoculars I spotted my first Herring Gull—and noticed that the people, a woman and three men, were fully and visibly naked. Jason apparently lives next to a nudist resort. It’s just like being in South Florida!
Two down, 58 to go. I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets, before venturing out into the huge map. My strategy for finding birds in GTA 6 was the same as finding birds in real life: look in as many habitats as I could find. I started by “borrowing” a fanboat off a nearby dock and heading back to the swampy areas near the seaplane mission. There were tons of birds across the open water and in the marsh: Caspian Terns, Mottled Ducks, Sanderlings, Spotted Sandpipers, Great Blue Herons, Glossy and White Ibis, and … flocks of Whooping Cranes?
incredibly healthy populations of critically-endangered Whooping Cranes across Vice City. Huge if true. https://t.co/doe6oMOvBX
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
In fact, I found a number of avian inaccuracies in just my first few hours of playtime. Certain species like Whooping Crane and Red-cockaded Woodpecker are common throughout the map, despite being endangered and threatened, respectively, in real life. Golden Eagles are extremely rare in Florida, but I found one soaring over the Mt. Kalaga area (mountains, one may point out, aren’t found in Florida either). Some species have confusing naming quirks—the chickadee is Black-capped instead of Carolina, and there’s a “New World Oriole” instead of a Baltimore Oriole—but those changes are likely due to the fact that Carolina and Baltimore don’t exist in the GTA universe.
Though some of the inaccuracies may feel like a letdown in a game that is being hailed as the Greatest of All Time, I think it’s important to remember that it’s also game where you can get a ride from a dog driving a jet ski. Grand Theft Auto games are meant to be fun, not science. Plus, despite some of the misfires, the avifauna feels well thought-out. The map is true to the ecological boundaries of South Florida, with herons, gulls, and other waterbirds in the south while birds like Red-bellied Woodpecker, Wood Stork, and American Robin are found farther north. Birders know that certain exotic species have made their home in tropical South Florida, including Spot-breasted Oriole and Red Junglefowl, both in the game.
That geographic fidelity is the main tip for anyone looking to check off all the game’s birds: Find their habitat. The game doesn’t tell you what species to look for, so you’ll need to cover a lot of ground to find everything. Wading birds, shorebirds, and seabirds are common in the southern coastal part of the map. A number of smaller, open-country or forest birds are found up north. Owls come out at night. Birds in zoos and domestic farmyard birds count towards the 60, too, so don’t overlook those areas.
Wild Boar roadkill. It’s just like birding in Florida! https://t.co/gT84IticOK
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
The most accurate aspect is the actual landscape. Having birded extensively across South Florida myself, the habitats are immediately recognizable, from the pebbly mangrove beaches at the Keys to the grassy swamps further north. The setting feels absolutely real, from the fonts on the roadside fruit stands to the roadkill alongside the highways. (I found dead wild boar and dead deer by the side of the road, and a Turkey Vulture somehow flew into a building I was in and died at my feet.) 
So, if you’re up for the kind of funhouse-mirror version of Florida that the game presents, you can have a blast, and adding birdwatching into the insane free-for-all makes for some delightful moments. This guy just wanted to look at a gull but ended up chucking a woman off a pier. I’ve made myself laugh out loud by screeching to a halt in the middle of busy highways or intersections and jumping out of my car to look for birds while motorist behind me scream and swear. I love it.
easily my favorite thing to do so far is just screech to a halt in the middle of a busy intersection and start birding https://t.co/QsDOLmNfYq
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026
As I was dodging dirt-biking rednecks to look for species in a northerly forest, I couldn’t help but compare birding in GTA 6 to birding in Red Dead Redemption 2 (RDR2), the latest installment in Rockstar’s other huge franchise. Birds and birding are presented quite similarly in both games, including the binocular “study” mechanic and many of the same species, but the experiences are totally different. RDR2 was set in the late 1800s, and players rode on horseback or locomotive through a comparatively wide-open and untrammeled version of America. There was mayhem in that game, too—outlaw gangs and marauders—but there were many peaceful moments, too, when a player could look out across wild landscape with nothing but nature as a soundtrack.
Not so in GTA 6. There’s plenty of birdsong on the soundtrack, but it competes with an endless racket of car radios, revving engines, swearing pedestrians, and blaring horns. There’s garbage almost everywhere, lapping the shorelines and blowing along the streets. There seems to be no inch of landscape in GTA 6 that hasn’t been lessened by the touch of humans. It is, I have to admit, a realistic depiction of birding in South Florida.
Birders working to fill out their GTA VI wildlife checklists should know something I just found out: THERE’S A ZOO https://t.co/2xN0joPKcR
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 20, 2026
Though GTA 6 provides what feels the most accurate version of modern birding ever put to screen, obsessing over the realism misses the point of having fun. Birders can, and should, visit the real South Florida to find the actual birds depicted in the game (and many more), but they can’t do it while also jumping over broken highway bridges on a stolen motorcycle. Birding is a bonus in GTA 6; mayhem is the draw.
I played for two hours after midnight, then about six straight hours Thursday before having to call it quits to write this column. In that time I found 50 of the 60 species listed in the “birds” compendium. I jumped back in this morning before work and found a huge chunk of species at a zoo (makes sense!) and on a farm, then found the 60th and final, an American Barn Owl, on a water tank in a town in the north of the map. Success! 
The biggest thing I can confirm is that all 60 birds on this list are available immediately, without needing any story progression. In Red Dead Redemption 2, some bird species were only found in Guarma, only accessible later in the game
— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 20, 2026
I felt a wave of satisfaction, and while I’m not certain if I was the first one to find them all, when I posted about it, a Rockstar designer replied with, “History!” I’d met my goal, and celebrated in a way that only Grand Theft Auto games allow: by driving my car full speed off a cliff into the ocean.

articles.title: Testing Terraform with AWS Emulator
articles.body:
Testing Terraform with AWS Emulator
Terraform plan passes and shows all green and all the necessary resource changes. You trigger apply and... the job fails with some obscure error that a resource can't be changed. You open another pull request and try again. And perhaps you encounter an error again. Sounds familiar? I bet it does. I encountered issues like this so many times I'm afraid to count. But recently AWS released a new tool called Emulator that emulates actual AWS API endpoints. And it should be great for tasks just like that!
Defining the problem #
The problem with the difference between plan and apply jobs is that plan can't possibly emulate every actual API call against a live infrastructure. It's a safe assumption based on the static declarations we put into it – the order of application, the necessary parameters, the proper configuration values. These mock calls can't know for a fact that you already have a resource in AWS called "my-bucket-asdasdasd" or that you're trying to upgrade a PostgreSQL RDS instance from version 14 to version 18 without an explicit "apply immediately" flag. One may argue that one can always try to apply changes locally, but this kinda undermines the whole automation workflow. So what is the answer?
There are multiple tools that can emulate AWS services either partially or in full, but what they lack is the actual knowledge of the service architecture. It may be similar, but it won't be authentic, and sometimes this small difference may cause a lot of problems. After all, what can be the closest to an AWS API, if not the same AWS API, but ephemeral?
AWS Emulator #
The benefit of the AWS Emulator is that it's a self-contained binary (or Docker container) that can be utilized locally or in a CI workflow. This means the usual "Plan > Apply" terraform workflow changes to "Plan > Apply against mock AWS infrastructure to test the plan > Apply on actual AWS Infrastructure". This means slightly longer jobs, but if you're like me and apply jobs run on commits to the main branch after a PR, this saves you the hassle of creating a new branch just to fix the issue.
Running Terraform against local AWS Emulator #
Let's start with a local setup and see how we can utilize AWS Emulator with the actual Terraform code. All code is available in my example GitHub repository.
First up, installation. You can either install aws-emulator via package manager, or build it with Docker. I'll use Docker to keep my system clear of yet another package:
bash$ docker build -t aws-emulator .
$ docker images
IMAGE                 ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
aws-emulator:latest   3c8fdb957b45       1.24GB             0B          # wow it's chonky
$ docker run --rm -d -p 9297:9297 aws-emulator -a off
dcc416f234aaa3ec2966c9e8dcde7870f8d03057ec8a465cb8960617af82e501
$ docker logs dcc416f234aaa3ec2966c9e8dcde7870f8d03057ec8a465cb8960617af82e501
{"timestamp":"2026-11-12T14:51:16.261883Z","level":"INFO","fields":{"message":"aws-emulator emulator starting"},"target":"aws_emulator"}
This emulator collects usage and error telemetry: enabled (on by default; opt out any time); disable with EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off or [telemetry] enabled = false in /home/emulator/.aws/emulator/config.toml
{"timestamp":"2026-11-12T14:51:16.270635Z","level":"INFO","fields":{"message":"emulator server information","endpoint_url":"https://127.0.0.1:9297","health_check_url":"https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health","config_file":"/home/emulator/.aws/emulator/9297/config","ca_file":"/home/emulator/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem","java_truststore_file":"/home/emulator/.aws/emulator/9297/truststore.p12"},"target":"aws_emulator_server"}
{"timestamp":"2026-11-12T14:51:16.270655Z","level":"WARN","fields":{"message":"the emulator listens on 0.0.0.0, not loopback: other machines that can reach port 9297 can call it; bind 127.0.0.1 (-b 127.0.0.1) unless that is intended","bind_address":"0.0.0.0"},"target":"aws_emulator_server"}
{"timestamp":"2026-11-12T14:51:16.270659Z","level":"WARN","fields":{"message":"request authentication is off: the emulator accepts any request, signed or not; start it with -a on to require signatures","bind_address":"0.0.0.0"},"target":"aws_emulator_server"}
And it's up and running! In the example above I set the container to live without limits (official AWS documentation proposes to set memory and swap limits: --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g, but for local that's fine). I also disabled authorization (flag -a off) to simplify things a bit.
To be sure aws-emulator is up and running, let's query the admin endpoint:
bash$ curl -sk https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health
ok
Okay, fake AWS is live, let's deploy some infrastructure!
I created an example AWS stack for Terraform and will use it in this article. First, let's configure Terraform to act against aws-emulator and not real AWS APIs. providers.tf will look like this:
hclprovider "aws" {
  access_key = var.access_key
  secret_key = var.secret_key
  region     = var.region
  insecure = true # The emulator serves HTTPS with a self-signed certificate. Skip verification.
  s3_use_path_style = true   # The emulator uses one IP endpoint. Put the bucket name in the path.
  # Do not call the real AWS or the instance metadata service.
  skip_credentials_validation = true
  skip_metadata_api_check     = true
  skip_requesting_account_id  = true
  skip_region_validation      = true
  # Send every service to the emulator instead of AWS.
  endpoints {
    ec2        = var.emulator_endpoint
    lambda     = var.emulator_endpoint
    iam        = var.emulator_endpoint
    sts        = var.emulator_endpoint
    cloudwatch = var.emulator_endpoint
    logs       = var.emulator_endpoint
    events     = var.emulator_endpoint
    sns        = var.emulator_endpoint
  }
  default_tags {
    tags = var.tags
  }
}
The difference between actual live infrastructure and a fake one is that we set up a bunch of flags to allow insecure connections (perhaps turning authentication off wasn't actually simpler?) and we set up an endpoint for each service we use in the setup to an emulator endpoint, which lives in the local Docker container:
hcl# variables.tf
variable "emulator_endpoint" {
  description = "Base URL of the AWS Emulator"
  type        = string
  default     = "https://127.0.0.1:9297"
}
...
The rest of the configuration is as usual: resources, variables, modules (if any). Just what your project has.
Let's proceed and test our setup. (I'll omit full terraform output otherwise this article would be 3 kilometers long)
bash$ cd terraform/
$ terraform init
Initializing the backend...
...
Terraform has been successfully initialized!
...
$ terraform plan
...
Plan: 15 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Changes to Outputs:
  + alarm_name          = "ttwae-lambda-errors"
  + event_rule_arn      = (known after apply)
  + lambda_function_arn = (known after apply)
  + security_group_id   = (known after apply)
  + sns_topic_arn       = (known after apply)
  + subnet_id           = (known after apply)
  + vpc_id              = (known after apply)
Plan works! That's good to see, but not what we're here for. Still, a good sign. Now for the real test.
bash$ terraform apply --auto-approve
...
Apply complete! Resources: 15 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
Outputs:
alarm_name = "ttwae-lambda-errors"
event_rule_arn = "arn:aws:events:us-east-1:000000000000:rule/ttwae-schedule"
lambda_function_arn = "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:000000000000:function:ttwae-worker"
security_group_id = "sg-00000000000000085"
sns_topic_arn = "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:000000000000:ttwae-alarms"
subnet_id = "subnet-00000000000000089"
vpc_id = "vpc-00000000000000080"
And apply also works! Amazing!
Sadly, the running aws-emulator container doesn't show in its logs which API requests it receives and what's happening under the hood, but I guess the tool is good enough as it is.
When you're done, stop the container:
bash$ docker stop dcc416f234aaa3ec2966c9e8dcde7870f8d03057ec8a465cb8960617af82e501
A container started with --rm removes itself after stopping, so no additional cleanup is needed. And as for the emulator -- it stores its state in memory, so each container restart drops all record of previous actions and any stale state.
Running Terraform against AWS Emulator in CI pipeline #
Now for the real test: can we wrap the desired logic inside a CI pipeline? Let's think.
For successful invocation in the pipeline we will need almost everything the same, but we will be limited by time (the faster -- the better, and overall reasonable timeouts) and resources.
The workflow with terraform apply against aws-emulator is shown down below. For it I decided to try out package manager installation (builders are ephemeral anyway) and proper authentication. Full workflow with actual successful runs can be found in the example GitHub repository.
yaml---
name: terraform-against-emulator
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  terraform:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      EMULATOR_PORT: "9297"
      # Empty keys make the provider fall back to the shared credentials
      # file that the emulator writes. insecure=false verifies the
      # emulator cert through AWS_CA_BUNDLE
      TF_VAR_access_key: ""
      TF_VAR_secret_key: ""
      TF_VAR_insecure: "false"
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - name: Install the AWS Emulator
        run: |
          curl -fsSLo aws-emulator.deb \
            https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/aws-emulator_amd64.deb
          sudo apt-get install -y ./aws-emulator.deb
          aws-emulator -v
      - name: Start the emulator with signature checks on
        run: |
          nohup aws-emulator > /tmp/aws-emulator.log 2>&1 &
          echo "Waiting for the emulator to answer..."
          CA="$HOME/.aws/emulator/${EMULATOR_PORT}/ca.pem"
          for i in $(seq 30); do
            if [ -f "$CA" ] && curl -sf --cacert "$CA" \
                "https://127.0.0.1:${EMULATOR_PORT}/__admin/health" >/dev/null; then
              echo "Emulator is ready."
              exit 0
            fi
            sleep 1
          done
          echo "Emulator did not become ready." >&2
          cat /tmp/aws-emulator.log >&2
          exit 1
      - name: Point Terraform at the emulator credentials and certificate
        run: |
          DIR="$HOME/.aws/emulator/${EMULATOR_PORT}"
          {
            echo "AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=$DIR/emulator_credentials"
            echo "AWS_CONFIG_FILE=$DIR/config"
            echo "AWS_CA_BUNDLE=$DIR/ca.pem"
            echo "AWS_REGION=us-east-1"
            echo "AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1"
            echo "AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true"
            echo "AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true"
          } >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@dfe3c3f87815947d99a8997f908cb6525fc44e9e # v4.0.1
        with:
          terraform_wrapper: false
      - run: terraform -chdir=terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform -chdir=terraform validate
      - run: terraform -chdir=terraform plan -input=false
      - run: terraform -chdir=terraform apply -auto-approve -input=false
This is a crude excerpt of the actual glorious workflow file that outlines the most important steps: emulator installation, terraform setup, plan and apply. On the example terraform architecture the whole pipeline took 1m25s, which is okay in my opinion, but there is room for improvement: sprinkle some caching on top, leave validation, format check for local hooks, etc.
Running a deliberately failing apply job #
It's always nice when code someone wrote on the internet works from the start after you copy-paste it onto your machine. That's why I always run the described processes myself -- building, testing, fixing, retrying -- before publishing an article. But showing only the positive scenarios creates a false sense of trust in the tool.
Let's break something on purpose.
In the example codebase I added a variable that, when enabled, makes the stack try to deploy a resource with an erroneous declaration. It will pass the plan job, but fail on apply.
hclvariable "enable_failure_demo" {
  description = "Create a DynamoDB table with an invalid name."
  type        = bool
  default     = false
}
Setting this variable to true at runtime will break our stack. Let's see:
bash$ cd terraform/
$ terraform init
Initializing the backend...
...
$ terraform plan -var 'enable_failure_demo=true'
...
Plan: 16 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Changes to Outputs:
...
  + failure_demo_table_arn = (known after apply)
...
$ terraform apply -auto-approve -var 'enable_failure_demo=true'
...
╷
│ Error: creating AWS DynamoDB Table (ab): operation error DynamoDB: CreateTable, https response error StatusCode: 400, RequestID: 4TLD3XUB94783KNA4C76L8BEZ26UU8LS4IBN2IEKZJLAK4NMVTQ4, api error ValidationException: 1 validation error detected: Value 'ab' at 'tableName' failed to satisfy constraint: Member must have length greater than or equal to 3
│
│   with aws_dynamodb_table.bad_name[0],
│   on dynamodb.tf line 10, in resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "bad_name":
│   10: resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "bad_name" {
│
And there we have it. The exact issue that arises only against actual API calls and not during a plan job.
For scenarios exactly like this, the emulator is priceless.
Limitations and considerations #
AWS Emulator is AWESOME. I'm rarely that excited about new tools lately (mostly because almost all of them are near/about AI), but this one is just so good and scratches that exact itch I felt for so long.
Still, it's far from perfect.
For starters, it can't effectively emulate IAM policies and permission checks. This is a bummer, because permission validation is such a crucial step for production-ready security. Here's hoping that the tool will evolve further and it will be included in future updates.
Second, as a tool still a work-in-progress[1], its capabilities are quite limited. Even while writing the article I encountered several cases of 501 NotImplemented. It complicates things a bit if your infrastructure setup is huge and has a lot of quirks and weird configurations and super new services. Still, AWS releases new versions quite often, and they're quite open about Emulator limitations, which is nice.
And last, but not least, is telemetry. AWS is explicit that it gathers telemetry and what this telemetry includes. This is honest behaviour and I like that approach. They even allow you to disable the telemetry, which further increases my trust in this tool. I understand the rationale behind this functionality (the tool is actively developed, they need the data to understand usage patterns and what goes wrong), but in the age of constant surveillance from Big Tech at every corner it still raises a slight concern. But then again, for the ultra-paranoid folks the code is open source and can be rebuilt with telemetry torn out of it.
- As of the moment of writing this article, AWS Emulator has been live for 1 day. ↩︎

articles.title: Supposed Fired Rockstar Engineer Says GTAVI Makes Psychological Profiles
articles.body:
An anonymous poster on 4chan’s technology board, claiming to be a former senior engine engineer at Rockstar North, alleges that GTA VI feeds granular gameplay data into an internal Take-Two system called “Lens,” which then generates behavioral and psychological classifications for each player. The poster claims they were fired shortly before GTA VI’s launch, reported as November 19, 2026, though that timing cannot be independently confirmed. The level of detail in the post is reminiscent of other cases of apps secretly tracking users without meaningful disclosure.
The poster’s identity and claimed employment at Rockstar North could not be verified from the available evidence. Nothing else in the account has been independently authenticated.
What the Post Actually Claims
The anonymous post describes a data collection system that goes well beyond what standard game telemetry typically involves.
According to the post, “Lens” allegedly captures controller input timing, analog stick movement patterns, reaction speed, and PS5 adaptive trigger pressure readings. From that raw data, the post claims the system generates scores or classifications across several behavioral dimensions.
The alleged categories, as described in the anonymous post, include impulse control, risk tolerance, aggression, patience, decision-making under pressure, and spending behavior.
Where the Data Allegedly Goes Next
The poster’s claims extend beyond data collection to describe a commercial data-sharing arrangement that remains entirely unconfirmed.
The account further alleges that this profiled data flows to a Delaware-incorporated company called “Vantage Analytics.” The poster describes it as a behavioral-AI business that licenses predictive models to insurers, credit-risk companies, HR platforms, and advertising brokers. This kind of commercial profiling pipeline echoes the methods documented in cases involving a surveillance app built to target specific population segments.
Available reporting found no reference to “Vantage Analytics” in reviewed Take-Two corporate filings, including an examination of approximately 145 listed subsidiaries in a Take-Two SEC filing. Its existence, role, and any connection to Take-Two remain unconfirmed. No response from Rockstar Games or Take-Two Interactive was identified in the reporting reviewed as of publication, and that absence of comment neither confirms nor refutes the claims.
The Verification Problem
The allegation occupies an uncomfortable space: specific enough to sound credible, and unsourced enough to require serious skepticism.
What makes it worth examining is that the technical language is coherent and internally consistent. The gaming industry does collect extensive telemetry, behavioral modeling is a real discipline, and data brokerage is a documented industry. A senior engine engineer with visibility into telemetry pipelines would at least be a plausible position from which to observe such a system, if one existed.
What creates serious doubt is the complete absence of corroboration. The post originated on 4chan and spread through 8kun, Reddit, and social media, all low-verification environments by nature. No independent confirmation was identified in the reporting reviewed. No documentation has been authenticated, and no second source has emerged. The allegation’s forum origins are not evidence that it is false, but they are a significant reason to withhold judgment.
Standard Telemetry Versus What This Alleges
Understanding what ordinary game telemetry looks like helps clarify why this allegation, if accurate, would represent something categorically different.
Developers routinely collect crash reports, playtime data, feature usage statistics, and performance metrics. That data is generally disclosed in privacy policies and used to improve software. Trends across the gaming industry suggest increasing scrutiny of how studios handle player data.
What the anonymous poster alleges is substantially further-reaching: behavioral inference from inputs the post characterizes as biometric-adjacent, linked to a platform identifier, and reportedly licensed to external commercial clients. If proven, that would raise serious questions under data-protection frameworks such as GDPR and CCPA regarding consent, disclosure, and third-party data transfers. Those are implications of the allegation, not established facts, and any legal conclusion would require qualified privacy-law expertise and confirmed facts about jurisdiction and processing.
What Would Actually Establish This
Verifying or refuting this allegation requires specific reporting steps that have not yet occurred.
Necessary starting points include a corporate registry search for “Vantage Analytics” in Delaware and a close review of Take-Two’s privacy disclosures and data-sharing agreements. Independent technical analysis of GTA VI’s network traffic and direct comment from Rockstar and Take-Two are also required, though network analysis alone may not reveal server-side processing or identify every legal entity receiving data.
Corroboration from additional named sources and input from a qualified privacy lawyer or data-governance expert would strengthen any further reporting considerably. Without those elements, no responsible conclusion about the allegation’s truth can be drawn.
Where Things Stand
A detailed, technically fluent allegation about GTA VI’s data collection is circulating online, and its evidentiary status remains unknown.
No independent confirmation was identified in the reporting reviewed. No response from Rockstar or Take-Two was on record as of publication. The source is anonymous and unauthenticated.
None of that means the claim is false. It means the honest answer right now is: unknown. Watch for official statements, independent technical analysis, and any corporate registry findings related to the entities named in the post. Until then, this is a claim worth monitoring , not unlike the controversies that have surrounded video games throughout their history , not a story already told.

articles.title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
articles.body:
Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
Raph Levien, November 21, 2026
This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.
Rust GUI is still compelling
The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.
Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.
The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?
For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.
Native is complicated
My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria.
I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.
While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.
Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" plan for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.
That said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.
Text layout and accessibility infrastructure is basically solved
One of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.
AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.
System compositor is still unsolved
One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.
There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.
This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.
Immediate vs retained mode
One of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.
That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.
For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.
Clearly defined modules
One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.
This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.
I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.
Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.
That said, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.
The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.
Blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.
One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.
By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.
Optimization opportunities
Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.
One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.
Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating new layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).
For a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.
Advice
- Be bold. Now is the time. Rust UI has the potential to deliver vastly higher performance than the status quo.
- Build on solid foundations.
- Use well-defined specs when available.
- Find ways to work well with open source. Work with upstream but don’t spam them with slop PRs.
Acknowledgements
Thanks to Nico Burns for reviewing an earlier draft of this post.
