articles.title: Blackberry releases secure browser for Windows
articles.body:
Introducing BlackBerry Access Secure Browser for Windows
The browser in the workplace: who governs yours?
Nov 20, 2026
·
Blog
·
Baldeep Dogra
Listen to this article
Somewhere in your organization, work is being done in a browser tab on a machine you do not own.
Most of what people do all day, from reading mail and joining meetings to approving cases and opening shared documents, now happens in a browser. The browser has become the way into the workplace.
That raises a question most organizations have never had to answer. On any device that touches corporate data, the browser now carries most of the work, and on a personal laptop, it may be the only part of the environment the organization can legitimately govern. So, who governs it? Who stops a user copying a link from a work email into their personal browser?
BlackBerry® Access Secure Browser for Windows is now available (link below). Built on Chromium, it brings BlackBerry data protection to the browser. It joins BlackBerry Access on iOS and Android and replaces the older BlackBerry Access desktop client.
An Access Problem Nobody Budgets for
Every organization has people it cannot practically equip, such as contractors on short engagements, staff at partner agencies, and employees working from their own machine rather than one the organization issued. The usual answer has been to ship managed hardware. The full cost is rarely counted: procurement, imaging, shipping, recovery at the end of the engagement, and the weeks before anyone can start work.
A governed browser answers the same question differently. It turns an unmanaged Windows PC into a usable route to internal applications without making it a managed device.
What About BYOD?
Bring your own device (BYOD) has always involved a trade-off. The organization gets greater flexibility and lower hardware costs; the user accepts some management on a personal machine. On phones that trade-off is tolerable, because work profiles and containers are well understood and the intrusion has limits. On personal laptops, that model is much harder to make work. People will not accept a management agent on the computer their family uses, and organizations are right to be wary of the liability that comes with putting one there.
The browser changes the unit being governed. Instead of managing the device, the organization governs the window through which work happens. Nothing outside the browser is touched. There is no agent, no claim on the user's photographs or personal files, and no remote wipe of a machine the organization never bought.
This is a narrower proposition than classic BYOD. Users accept it because it limits the organization's control to the work it can legitimately govern on someone else's property. A control only works if people use it. When controls make work harder, people find ways around them.
Doing the Work on a Personal PC, Not Just Reaching It
Access on a personal machine is only useful if people can work there. Outlook, Teams, and OneDrive run as progressive web apps (web apps that install with their own desktop icon and window), and Teams provides native Windows notifications. Users get an experience close to a corporate build without needing one.
Users reach internal web applications through BlackBerry connectivity infrastructure, with no VPN client. For organizations that hit VPN capacity limits, or whose VPN fails during an incident, this gives a second route that does not depend on the first. Some customers run it as a fallback alongside their VPN rather than as a replacement.
Downloaded files stay in protected storage inside BlackBerry Access instead of landing on the PC as ordinary files. An integrated LibreOffice component lets users edit documents offline, on a train or over a poor hotel connection.
Where Many Secure Browsers Fall Short for Government
Secure browsers have become increasingly capable, but most rely on a vendor-operated cloud control plane to set browser policy and collect activity data.
For many commercial enterprises, that may not be a deciding factor. For government agencies, regulators, and critical infrastructure operators, it can be. For these organizations, the questions are different: Who controls browser policy? Where is that control exercised? And under whose legal jurisdiction?
BlackBerry Access is a BlackBerry® Dynamics™ application that runs in an encrypted container and inherits the deployment model of BlackBerry UEM. When BlackBerry UEM is deployed on premises, browser policy, management, and identity remain within the organization's own environment and jurisdiction. For organizations with stricter sovereignty requirements, the same technology can also operate on an air-gapped network.
This has legal weight. Under the EU General Data Protection Regulation, the European Data Protection Board treats remote access to personal data from outside the EU as a transfer, even when the data itself stays inside the EU (EDPB Guidelines 05/2021). In practice, if a browser is controlled from a vendor's cloud outside the EU, that remote control can count as a data transfer under GDPR. If the same browser is controlled from a console the organization runs on its own premises, no such transfer occurs.
That can open up use cases that a foreign-operated control plane may complicate or rule out. A contractor might securely access sensitive organizational resources from a personal device. Partner ministries might access a shared application during a joint operation. And an agency can retain control of browser policy within its own jurisdiction.
Sovereign browsers may not yet be an established analyst category, but the requirement already exists. For organizations that need to control not only their data but also the infrastructure governing access to it, where the browser is managed matters. BlackBerry Access addresses that requirement by allowing organizations to keep browser policy and identity on infrastructure they control.

articles.title: Quantum Computing's First Real-world Payoff May Come In Energy Solutions
articles.body:
Quantum Computing's First Real-world Payoff May Come In Energy Solutions (cnbc.com) 23
			
		 	
				While quantum computing's biggest breakthroughs "are still likely to be years, if not decades, away," CNBC reports the technology is already being tested in energy applications, "from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production."
Quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture.  Another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently...  For [quantum software company] Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator, the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The company says its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing... 
[Phasecraft] is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones.  Separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen. Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, [cofounder/CEO Ashley] Montanaro said the returns were there too.  "When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he said.

articles.title: GTA 6: 32.5 Million copies, Cameos, and Easter Eggs - but No Physical Discs
articles.body:
GTA 6: 32.5 Million copies, Cameos, and Easter Eggs - but No Physical Discs (yahoo.com) 30
			
		 	
				Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News, which is liveblogging all the videogame history happening after GTA 6's Thursday launch. 
Like how singer The Weeknd says he found his real-life mansion appearing in the game... How players found a glitch that apparently lets you override the game's third-person point of view to play in first-person.   And apparently it's also possible to jack an old woman's mobility scooter.  (Though it makes for a very slow getaway, it's reportedly the GTA 6 vehicle that's least likely to crash...)
- The jet-skiing dog in 'GTA 6' appears to be based on a real Florida dog.  Swim too far out to sea in GTA 6 and a dog in goggles and a life jacket will come to the rescue on a jet ski...  Florida locals quickly recognized it. The dog appears to be a nod to Loosy, a golden retriever from Fort Lauderdale who went viral in May riding a jet ski down the New River while her owner, Eddie Inch, towed her along on a jet-powered hoverboard... 
— GTA 6 isn't approved for sale in mainland China, but that hasn't stopped gamers from getting their hands on it — or Rockstar Games from promoting it there [Reuters reports]. The developer has been pushing the blockbuster game on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, despite the country's strict rules on violent video games.   Meanwhile, Business Insider reports that Chinese gamers are circumventing the restrictions by using imported consoles and overseas digital stores.   Zac Ling, a project manager at Shanghai-based consultancy Daxue Consulting, said gamers in mainland China could buy 3 million to 5 million copies of the game in its first week.   The game's graphic content has also prompted censorship in Japan, according to IGN. 
- Beloved '80s song parody writer and GTA fan "Weird" Al Yankovic said Thursday that he's the host of the non-stop '80s radio channel Vice City FM in GTA 6. In social media posts, Yankovic said he also wrote some of the in-game commercials and voices the Burger Shot ads.
 
Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News.    Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels, according to the BBC.  And "New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access."  At its peak, nearly 8 million people were watching GTA 6 livestreams at the same time, Axios reported.  PlayStation's network suffered a brief outage Wednesday afternoon as the game became available and players made the required update to their consoles. But since Wednesday evening, it's been smooth sailing. [Around 75% of Grand Theft Auto VI sales have been on PlayStation 5, with the rest on Xbox, the BBC reported, citing estimates from analytics firm Sensor Tower.]	
Yahoo news shares lots of crazy stories about GTA 6's world-building, like its cameos of real-world celebrities, its in-game hiking trails, and the way a GTA 6 house Rockstar first teased in 2021 hides a conspiracy-minded NPC who's convinced that he's in a video game.
But they note that GTA 6 also brings questions on how videogames are sold and accessed:
The game is being sold for $80 in boxes containing download codes instead of discs, meaning players can't trade in or resell their copies.  "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," [GameStop CEO Ryan] Cohen told Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop."  Cohen said the move away from physical games also reduces competition from the secondhand market.

articles.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
articles.body:
From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently(opens in a new window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1
I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared(opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.
A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.
The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.
The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.
As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.
A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.
We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.
Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.
Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:
- Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.
- Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.
- Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.
- Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.
At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.
Author
Footnotes
- 1
- 2
- 3
- 4 Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI.
- 5 On the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI.

Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.
Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:
- Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.
- Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.
- Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.
- Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.
At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.
Author
Footnotes
- 1
- 2
- 3
- 4 Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI.
- 5 On the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI.

articles.title: Norway to extend proposed under-16 social media ban to games and messaging apps
articles.body:
Online games and messaging services were initially expected to receive broad exemptions, but the government has now decided to assess platforms based on their potential risks to children.
Norway is set to introduce a social media ban for children under 16, with the government announcing on Monday that it is finalising legislation to be submitted to parliament by the end of the year.
The proposed restrictions will also cover potentially harmful online games and messaging services, beyond conventional social media platforms, the government said in a statement.
TikTok, Snapchat and Roblox, a popular online gaming platform where users can create and play games while interacting with others, would likely fall under the proposed law.
"Children's safety must come first," said Lene Vågslid, Norway's minister for children and families, adding that the legislation was nearly complete.
The restrictions aim to protect children from harmful content, addictive features, illegal advertising and unwanted contact from strangers.
Online games and messaging services were initially expected to receive broad exemptions, but the government has now decided to assess platforms based on their potential risks to children.
This means services considered harmless, such as messaging apps used for school communication, could remain accessible.
Vågslid said the government was also safeguarding children's "right to participate," although Monday's announcement did not explain how this would be ensured under the proposed restrictions.
Technology companies would be responsible for verifying users' ages, with systems required to comply with European data protection rules.
Norway's centre-left Labour government published a draft bill in 2025 proposing a minimum social media age of 15 before revising the threshold to 16 in April this year. The legislation has since undergone public consultation in Norway and the European Economic Area (EEA).
Social media restrictions in Europe
Norway joins a growing number of European countries moving to restrict children's access to social media amid concerns about online safety and addiction.
Denmark has adopted similar restrictions, while Spain is pursuing a ban for pupils under 16.
In September, France attempted to ban social media for children under 15, but its Constitutional Council struck it down over freedom of expression concerns.
At the European Union level, the European Commission proposed the EU Kids Act in September, which would also introduce age-based restrictions on social media, online games and other digital services.

articles.title: Fascism and Monopoly
articles.body:
Home > Journals > Michigan Law Review > MLR > Volume 118 > Issue 7 (2020)
Abstract
The recent revival of political interest in antitrust has resurfaced a longstanding debate about the role of industrial concentration and monopoly in enabling Hitler’s rise to power and the Third Reich’s wars of aggression. Proponents of stronger antitrust enforcement argue that monopolies and cartels brought the Nazis to power and warn that rising concentration in the American economy could similarly threaten democracy. Skeptics demur, observing that German big business largely opposed Hitler during the crucial years of his ascent. Drawing on business histories and archival material from the U.S. Office of Military Government’s Decartelization Branch, this Article assesses the historical record on the role of industrial concentration in facilitating Nazism. It finds compelling evidence that, while German big business principally did not support Hitler before he won the chancellorship in 1933, the extreme concentration of market power during the Weimar period enabled Hitler to seize and consolidate totalitarian power through a variety of mechanisms. Hence, the German experience with Nazism lends support to the idea that extreme concentration of economic power enables extreme concentration of political power. However, most of the conduct that created the radical economic concentration of the Weimar period would be unlawful under contemporary antitrust principles, which casts doubt on claims that a significant shift in antitrust enforcement is necessary to forestall antidemocratic forces.
Recommended Citation
    Daniel A. Crane,
    Fascism and Monopoly,
    118
    Mich. L. Rev.
    1315
        (2020).

articles.title: Harsher on Male? Evaluating LLMs on Gender-Asymmetric Moral Framing in Conflicts
articles.body:
Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 12 Jun 2026]
Title:Harsher on Male? Evaluating LLMs on Gender-Asymmetric Moral Framing Across Diverse Conflict Scenarios
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Existing studies on gender bias in LLMs have largely focused on stereotypes, occupational associations, or explicit harmful outputs. In this work, we ask whether LLMs apply consistent response standards to the same negative behavior under matched male-actor and female-actor conditions. We introduce GAMA-Bench, a gender-mirrored benchmark of 1,298 scenarios covering intimate relationship and public social conflicts. It constructs gender-neutral misconduct templates through controlled grids and cross-model review, then compiles them into paired first-person prompts with matched actor-gender and role-reference variations. We further design a structured response-framing protocol to measure how models allocate punishment, empathy, escalation, instruction, and blame. Experiments on 10 representative LLMs reveal a consistent male-disadvantaging asymmetry: male actors receive more punitive, escalatory, and blame-centered framing, whereas female actors receive more therapeutic and empathy-oriented framing for the same misconduct. Further analyses show that this pattern persists across model families, scenario tracks, model scale, and explicit thinking-style reasoning. The official code is available at this https URL.

articles.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
articles.body:
- Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News.
- The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.
- Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.
Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.
In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.
For Sale Near You
See all results for used Toyota for sale near 95123
The first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.
The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.
“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”
➡️ Skip the lot. Let Car and Driver help you find your next car.
Jack Fitzgerald’s love for cars stems from his as yet unshakable addiction to Formula 1. After a brief stint as a detailer for a local dealership group in college, he knew he needed a more permanent way to drive all the new cars he couldn’t afford and decided to pursue a career in auto writing. By hounding his college professors at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, he was able to travel Wisconsin seeking out stories in the auto world before landing his dream job at Car and Driver. His new goal is to delay the inevitable demise of his 2010 Volkswagen Golf.

articles.title: Notes on the discrete Fourier transform (DFT)
articles.body:
In the previous post on this topic, we’ve seen how the Discrete-Time Fourier Series (DTFS) and transform (DTFT) are used to analyze infinite-duration periodic and non-periodic discrete signals. Now, it’s time to turn to realistic digital signal processing where signals are not only discrete, but also finite in duration.
Analyzing signal samples
Suppose we have samples of a signal - it’s a list of numbers:
We want to analyze the frequencies present in this signal; in other words, to find the coefficients in a series of complex exponentials that reconstructs the signal. One option is to assume that is an infinite domain signal with zero values outside our samples, and then compute its DTFT:
However, this is a continuous function of frequency , so it’s difficult compute on an actual computer; we cannot evaluate and store it for all , so we have to choose which to compute it for. We'll soon see how this choice is made.
The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)
But there's an alternative way to look at the problem. We only have samples of the signal , so we can assume they represent a single period of a periodic signal. And in that case, we can use DTFS; recall that the coefficients of the series are:
As we’ve seen in the post on the DTFS, this series can be used to reconstruct a discrete, periodic signal precisely. Since our signal is finite and we assume it’s just one period of a periodic signal, it means we can also reconstruct precisely using a DTFS.
This is the main insight behind the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). First, by convention [1] we define:
And then:
This is called the Discrete Fourier Transform of . The term transform may be a bit puzzling here - after all, we’re just using the series coefficients - so isn’t it more proper to just say series? Perhaps, though in mathematics a transform has a pretty general meaning of "a mapping that takes a mathematical object and produces another object"; in that sense, "transform" is proper here because we take an object - and produce another object - .
Moreover, DFT and DTFT are intimately related. Recall how we said earlier that the DTFT is tricky to compute because is a continuous variable? Well, the DFT gives us a way to sample that variable into the discrete domain:
So the DFT can be seen as exactly equally spaced samples of the DTFT.
Computing the DFT
Since the goal of this post is specifically to demonstrate computable methods of applying Fourier analysis to discrete digital signals, here’s the Python code to calculate the DFT of a signal:
def dft(x):
    """Return X[k] = sum_n x[n] exp(-2 pi i k n / N)."""
    N = len(x)
    n = np.arange(N)
    X = np.empty(N, dtype=complex)
    for k in range(N):
        weights = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * k * n / N)
        X[k] = np.sum(x * weights)
    return X
It shouldn’t be hard to see the correspondence between this code and the mathematical formula for . Python’s Numpy code is vectorized by default, so the weights array is computed in whole for every k (because n is an array of indices ).
DFT and the complex roots of unity
In my earlier post on the complex roots of unity, we’ve seen how powers of the roots of unity form an orthogonal basis for . Now let’s show the beautiful theoretical connection between this fact and the DFT.
Recall that the -th roots of unity can be written as:
Since all are just powers of , we can write them as:
The conjugates of the roots of unity are roots of unity themselves:
With being the same as , so when we enumerate all the roots of unity, we’re also enumerating their conjugates, just in a reversed order.
With that in mind, let’s denote [2] , and examine the sequence:
The vectors formed by (element-wise) raising to integer powers from to can be collected into a matrix:
In the roots of unity post, we’ve proven that the rows of this matrix form an orthogonal basis over . In other words, any vector in can be represented as a linear combination of the rows of .
I hope you can see where this is going! Let’s consider the signal as a column vector in . The DFT of can be computed by multiplying by the matrix :
Take a minute to convince yourself this is true, by working through the multiplication for a specific row , e.g. is computed via row-column multiplication the third row (counting from 0) of and .
Our is called the Fourier Matrix or the DFT Matrix. Previously we’ve seen Python code that directly computes the DFT; here’s a version that does this via the matrix multiplication approach:
def dft_matrix(N):
    """Construct F[k, n] = W_N**(k*n), where W_N = exp(-2 pi i / N)."""
    # W_N is a primitive N-th root of unity: W_N**N = 1.
    # Its powers give all N roots of z**N - 1 = 0.
    root = np.exp(-2j * np.pi / N)
    indices = np.arange(N)
    # Rows correspond to frequency bins k; columns to sample indices n.
    exponents = np.outer(indices, indices)
    return root**exponents
def dft_via_matrix(x):
    """Compute the DFT as F @ x with the Fourier matrix"""
    return dft_matrix(len(x)) @ x
More than the computational convenience though, there’s theoretical elegance here. Back when we were discussing the continuous Fourier series, we’ve seen how the trigonometric functions (or - equivalently - complex exponentials) form an orthogonal basis for square integrable functions.
Here, we see a similar linear algebra connection in discrete time - the vectors formed from powers of complex roots of unity form an orthogonal basis in and can thus be used to represent any sequence of complex values.
Which brings us to the next topic: reconstructing a signal from its DFT representation.
Inverse DFT: reconstructing the signal
There are two equivalent approaches to find the inverse DFT - the formula we can use to reconstruct given . The first approach is going back to DTFS, where the reconstruction formula is:
Recall that our convention is . Therefore:
This is the Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform formula.
Let’s examine the other approach now, because it uses our linear algebra interpretation in an enlightening way.
Recall the Fourier matrix , and consider - the same matrix where every element is the conjugate of the corresponding element of . If:
Then:
What happens if we multiply by ?
We have seen in the roots of unity post that this amounts to:
In other words:
Where is the identity matrix. Since is a square matrix, any matrix that multiplies with it to give the identity is its inverse:
Recall that in vector form:
Therefore:
With our definition of :
And in sum form:
Which is the same reconstruction formula we obtained from the DTFS. In mathematics, it’s always a good sign when we obtain the same result using different methods!
The linear algebra interpretation here is clear: the vectors formed by the powers of roots of unity form an orthogonal basis over . Therefore, every vector can be represented as a linear combination of these vectors. Moreover, this transformation is invertible, and the original vector can be reconstructed by left-multiplying its DFT vector by .
Example
It’s time for a fully worked example; the entire Python code for this example is available on GitHub; read through its main function, which is well commented.
Recall the sampled triangular signal we’ve used in the previous post; here, let’s use a single cycle:
In code, this is just an array of numbers:
x = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3, -2, -1]) / 3
Calculating the DFT of this signal using the code shown earlier produces the following values; remember that consists of complex numbers, so we represent them as a magnitude-phase pair. Phase is only shown for nonzero coefficients, because the phase of zero is undefined [3]:
Obviously, we’d get exactly the same numbers by using the matrix multiplication method of computing the DFT. And to reconstruct the signal, we multiply by the computed IDFT matrix to get the original signal back. The reconstruction matches the original signal precisely, with any differences being attributable to floating point round-off.
Efficiently computing the DFT
The sample code contains another method of computing the DFT of this signal - by calling NumPy’s fft.fft function. This refers to the Fast Fourier Transform, which is considered to be one of the most important algorithms of the 20th century. By exploiting the structure of the Fourier matrix , FFT computes the product in operations, compared with for direct matrix-vector multiplication. I plan to cover how this works in a future post.
Appendix: spectral leakage
Looking carefully at the signal used in the Example section above, we see that it’s actually one full cycle out of a sampled triangle wave. This is convenient, because repeating the block reproduces the original triangle wave. But what happens when the samples cover only part of the cycle?
Take for example just the first 10 samples of the triangle wave:
If we naively extend this signal periodically, things won’t line up (there will be a jump at the end of every cycle). We can still calculate its DFT, of course; these are the coefficients we’ll get:
While the coefficients still come in conjugate pairs (because the samples are real), the original triangle’s frequencies no longer coincide with the DFT’s frequency bins, so their contributions spread across multiple bins. This is called spectral leakage.
By applying the IDFT we can still reconstruct the original 10-sample signal perfectly! So if all we need is reconstruction, spectral leakage isn’t an issue; but if we’re doing frequency analysis, it skews the situation somewhat, adding frequencies that didn’t really exist in the underlying triangle wave - just to account for the discontinuity. In real-world signal processing, such issues are usually addressed by applying special window functions to the signal after sampling - these help alleviate leakage by tapering the signal close to zero at the edges.

As we’ve seen in the post on the DTFS, this series can be used to reconstruct a discrete, periodic signal precisely. Since our signal is finite and we assume it’s just one period of a periodic signal, it means we can also reconstruct precisely using a DTFS.
This is the main insight behind the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). First, by convention [1] we define:
And then:
This is called the Discrete Fourier Transform of . The term transform may be a bit puzzling here - after all, we’re just using the series coefficients - so isn’t it more proper to just say series? Perhaps, though in mathematics a transform has a pretty general meaning of "a mapping that takes a mathematical object and produces another object"; in that sense, "transform" is proper here because we take an object - and produce another object - .
Moreover, DFT and DTFT are intimately related. Recall how we said earlier that the DTFT is tricky to compute because is a continuous variable? Well, the DFT gives us a way to sample that variable into the discrete domain:
So the DFT can be seen as exactly equally spaced samples of the DTFT.
Computing the DFT
Since the goal of this post is specifically to demonstrate computable methods of applying Fourier analysis to discrete digital signals, here’s the Python code to calculate the DFT of a signal:
def dft(x):
    """Return X[k] = sum_n x[n] exp(-2 pi i k n / N)."""
    N = len(x)
    n = np.arange(N)
    X = np.empty(N, dtype=complex)
    for k in range(N):
        weights = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * k * n / N)
        X[k] = np.sum(x * weights)
    return X
It shouldn’t be hard to see the correspondence between this code and the mathematical formula for . Python’s Numpy code is vectorized by default, so the weights array is computed in whole for every k (because n is an array of indices ).
DFT and the complex roots of unity
In my earlier post on the complex roots of unity, we’ve seen how powers of the roots of unity form an orthogonal basis for . Now let’s show the beautiful theoretical connection between this fact and the DFT.
Recall that the -th roots of unity can be written as:
Since all are just powers of , we can write them as:
The conjugates of the roots of unity are roots of unity themselves:
With being the same as , so when we enumerate all the roots of unity, we’re also enumerating their conjugates, just in a reversed order.
With that in mind, let’s denote [2] , and examine the sequence:
The vectors formed by (element-wise) raising to integer powers from to can be collected into a matrix:
In the roots of unity post, we’ve proven that the rows of this matrix form an orthogonal basis over . In other words, any vector in can be represented as a linear combination of the rows of .
I hope you can see where this is going! Let’s consider the signal as a column vector in . The DFT of can be computed by multiplying by the matrix :
Take a minute to convince yourself this is true, by working through the multiplication for a specific row , e.g. is computed via row-column multiplication the third row (counting from 0) of and .
Our is called the Fourier Matrix or the DFT Matrix. Previously we’ve seen Python code that directly computes the DFT; here’s a version that does this via the matrix multiplication approach:
def dft_matrix(N):
    """Construct F[k, n] = W_N**(k*n), where W_N = exp(-2 pi i / N)."""
    # W_N is a primitive N-th root of unity: W_N**N = 1.
    # Its powers give all N roots of z**N - 1 = 0.
    root = np.exp(-2j * np.pi / N)
    indices = np.arange(N)
    # Rows correspond to frequency bins k; columns to sample indices n.
    exponents = np.outer(indices, indices)
    return root**exponents
def dft_via_matrix(x):
    """Compute the DFT as F @ x with the Fourier matrix"""
    return dft_matrix(len(x)) @ x
More than the computational convenience though, there’s theoretical elegance here. Back when we were discussing the continuous Fourier series, we’ve seen how the trigonometric functions (or - equivalently - complex exponentials) form an orthogonal basis for square integrable functions.
Here, we see a similar linear algebra connection in discrete time - the vectors formed from powers of complex roots of unity form an orthogonal basis in and can thus be used to represent any sequence of complex values.
Which brings us to the next topic: reconstructing a signal from its DFT representation.
Inverse DFT: reconstructing the signal
There are two equivalent approaches to find the inverse DFT - the formula we can use to reconstruct given . The first approach is going back to DTFS, where the reconstruction formula is:
Recall that our convention is . Therefore:
This is the Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform formula.
Let’s examine the other approach now, because it uses our linear algebra interpretation in an enlightening way.
Recall the Fourier matrix , and consider - the same matrix where every element is the conjugate of the corresponding element of . If:
Then:
What happens if we multiply by ?
We have seen in the roots of unity post that this amounts to:
In other words:
Where is the identity matrix. Since is a square matrix, any matrix that multiplies with it to give the identity is its inverse:
Recall that in vector form:
Therefore:
With our definition of :
And in sum form:
Which is the same reconstruction formula we obtained from the DTFS. In mathematics, it’s always a good sign when we obtain the same result using different methods!
The linear algebra interpretation here is clear: the vectors formed by the powers of roots of unity form an orthogonal basis over . Therefore, every vector can be represented as a linear combination of these vectors. Moreover, this transformation is invertible, and the original vector can be reconstructed by left-multiplying its DFT vector by .
Example
It’s time for a fully worked example; the entire Python code for this example is available on GitHub; read through its main function, which is well commented.
Recall the sampled triangular signal we’ve used in the previous post; here, let’s use a single cycle:
In code, this is just an array of numbers:
x = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3, -2, -1]) / 3
Calculating the DFT of this signal using the code shown earlier produces the following values; remember that consists of complex numbers, so we represent them as a magnitude-phase pair. Phase is only shown for nonzero coefficients, because the phase of zero is undefined [3]:
Obviously, we’d get exactly the same numbers by using the matrix multiplication method of computing the DFT. And to reconstruct the signal, we multiply by the computed IDFT matrix to get the original signal back. The reconstruction matches the original signal precisely, with any differences being attributable to floating point round-off.
Efficiently computing the DFT
The sample code contains another method of computing the DFT of this signal - by calling NumPy’s fft.fft function. This refers to the Fast Fourier Transform, which is considered to be one of the most important algorithms of the 20th century. By exploiting the structure of the Fourier matrix , FFT computes the product in operations, compared with for direct matrix-vector multiplication. I plan to cover how this works in a future post.
Appendix: spectral leakage
Looking carefully at the signal used in the Example section above, we see that it’s actually one full cycle out of a sampled triangle wave. This is convenient, because repeating the block reproduces the original triangle wave. But what happens when the samples cover only part of the cycle?
Take for example just the first 10 samples of the triangle wave:
If we naively extend this signal periodically, things won’t line up (there will be a jump at the end of every cycle). We can still calculate its DFT, of course; these are the coefficients we’ll get:
While the coefficients still come in conjugate pairs (because the samples are real), the original triangle’s frequencies no longer coincide with the DFT’s frequency bins, so their contributions spread across multiple bins. This is called spectral leakage.
By applying the IDFT we can still reconstruct the original 10-sample signal perfectly! So if all we need is reconstruction, spectral leakage isn’t an issue; but if we’re doing frequency analysis, it skews the situation somewhat, adding frequencies that didn’t really exist in the underlying triangle wave - just to account for the discontinuity. In real-world signal processing, such issues are usually addressed by applying special window functions to the signal after sampling - these help alleviate leakage by tapering the signal close to zero at the edges.

articles.title: Python Devs Document 'De-fanging Dangerous Triggers In GitHub Actions'
articles.body:
Python Devs Document 'De-fanging Dangerous Triggers In GitHub Actions' (blogspot.com)
			
		 	
				"A handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets," warn two security developers at the Python Software Foundation.
Have dangerous triggers caused real incidents?  Yes, repeatedly... The maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one...
When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. That's the safe one.   pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets. GitHub built it for chores like labeling pull requests from forks, where the workflow never touches the contributor's code. The trouble starts when a workflow checks out the pull request and runs it anyway...  Anyone with a GitHub account can open that pull request. Their code now runs with your credentials. This is called a "pwn request", and GitHub's docs describe it as the root cause of multiple supply-chain compromises.   
The issue_comment trigger carries the same risk. This trigger fires when anyone comments on an issue or pull request, and the workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets...  Sometimes the workflow pastes the comment text into a templated shell command, and the comment turns out to inject different instructions into the workflow shell.
 
Python's official security developer in residence Seth Larson joined PyPI safety/security engineer Mike Fiedler
to remove these dangerous trigger, also applying the policies Python Software Foundation-stewarded GitHub organizations (psf, python, and pypi).   "They also wrote up technical documentation on how to roll these policies out to your own projects and organizations.
"On a GitHub Team or Enterprise plan, you can turn them off for every repository in your organization with one policy. On a Free plan, you can do it one repository at a time. Set the policy up, check what it would block, then enforce it."

articles.title: Several Waymo Self-Driving Cars Stalled in Traffic as San Francisco's Streets Flooded
articles.body:
Several Waymo Self-Driving Cars Stalled in Traffic as San Francisco's Streets Flooded (sfist.com) 69
			
		 	
				San Francisco's streets flooded this week after heavy rainfall — confusing several Waymo self-driving cars. The San Francisco blog Sfist describes what happened after the flooding in some places rose as high as three feet:
Two lanes of Oak Street by the Golden Gate Park Panhandle were flooded Wednesday morning, with water spouting out of manhole covers, leading to a traffic backup that was made worse by a Waymo that couldn't figure its way out of the situation. The Waymo vehicle came to a stop in front of the spouting water, blocking one of the only passable lanes and worsening the traffic situation, as seen in the video below that is going viral...  ["Other drivers had to veer into deeper water to weave around it," reports the San Francisco Chronicle.]
Elsewhere in the city, Waymo rider Edward Frazer posted the video below to X, also around 10:20 am, saying that he had been in a Waymo for an hour and a half trying to get from North Beach to Mission Bay, with the vehicle pulling over around 10 times as it encountered flooded streets. The video shows the Waymo on what appears to be Townsend Street near Adobe's headquarters, stalled as water puddles in front of it. 
Waymo subsequently suspended all service for the rest of the day. 
But "frozen robotaxis were already clogging San Francisco streets by the time Waymo decided to rein in the fleet," reports the San Francisco Chronicle:
 Rider Amy Gutierrez said her Waymo suddenly stopped on Fell Street at the intersection of Masonic Avenue, where rain was coursing into rivers. She contacted company support and was transferred to three specialists who tried to move the jammed vehicle.   It took a half-hour of false starts before they managed to remotely maneuver it to the right lane.  "We were kind of just stuck there — cars were honking," she said, and other drivers were frustrated as traffic backed up. "One person drove by smacking their window, like 'Get out of the way.'" 
Or, as the New York Post puts it, "Waymos spark terror as they trap drivers in rapidly rising floodwater as monster storm hits California city."
Waymos have sparked chaos in San Francisco as they trapped passengers in cars despite rapidly rising floods.  Multiple self-driving vehicles were paralyzed across the streets and left those inside frantically calling the company to help get them to safety.
One was trapped in the middle of a busy intersection when the car refused to go around an overflowing drain, leaving other drivers to go on the wrong side of the road to get around.... 
The San Francisco Chronicle also remembers that last year's power blackout caused 1,600 Waymo vehicles to stall "because they required a 'confirmation check' from a human operator before navigating stoplights after the power was cut. Hundreds of requests overwhelmed the system, leaving San Francisco streets full of paralyzed self-driving vehicles."
Thanks to Slashdot reader AzWa Snowbird for sharing the news.

articles.title: Was software just always too complex for humans?
articles.body:
I was glued to the Lean chat as the legendary Riemann hypothesis was cracked via 17 million (!) lines of AI-assisted code last week. This has since been certified correct despite no human (yet) understanding how it works. The future of maths, and much science, is clearly going to involve human-AI boosting.
However, it also struck me deeply just how broken software engineering has been for my entire life! There's always been an imbalance between our understanding of the theory of computation and our relentless drive to deploy software throughout society. We're paying the piper now as all those decades of human-written code turn out to be full of bugs. Since software essentially drives society now, weird things happen like supermarket fridges needing James Bond to secure them. This has led to people like Tim Gowers joining the Pause AI march.
How the hell did we get here? Have we just completely overestimated the human ability to write software? Or will software engineering 'catch up' once LLM harnesses get better?
Software was reasonably under control in pre-AI times when attackers were roughly symmetric with defenders, but all the recent mysteriously correlated outages and disclosed issues (Java, PHP, Linux) all point to an acceleration of security pain in 2027. I only see two ways this can go...
1 Derive everything from specifications
In April this year, I couldn't believe we'd ever formally specify every layer of hardware and software:
I find it hard to believe that we will formally specify all layers of hardware and software and roll them out into production...ever. A Fire Upon the Deep's software archeologists are a profession that's here today and not a scifi trope. -- The Internet needs an antibotty immune system, stat, April 2026
How a few months makes a difference. With the pace of frontier model advances, translating the vast body of existing legacy code seems entirely plausible if we first speedrun towards defining formal specifications for all of our services, and derive all new software from those as well.
That means rebuilding operating system stacks from the ground up and even reengineering instruction sets to match. There are terrible legacy interfaces throughout the stack, largely because our software layers grew so that human groups could scale working on different parts. Other approaches do make it easier though. Unikernels with a libOS linking discipline plus shared memory interconnects are remarkably composable and allow agents to specialise the whole stack at link time, with fewer interfaces making the specification task less daunting.
Having good specs also conveniently takes humans out of the security response patch loop. Attackers are currently bounded only by their desire to break in somewhere, while defenders have to wait on maintainer triage. However, fixes re-derived from a formal spec and machine-checked could work more reliably in a timely fashion. The human job remains writing the interfaces iteratively with an AI.
2 Engineer diversity in deliberately
Historically, software has tended towards a monoculture through reuse, so one bug can screw over vast numbers of hosts. Agents could instead force diversity via novel 'genetic' mechanisms so digital services aren't all simultaneously infected. This works well with formal specifications, since any decent spec allows multiple valid implementations. The Internet's entire philosophy is based around Postel's Law and encouraging hosts to be liberal in what we receive and strict in what we transmit.
The catch, of course, is having just a handful of gated frontier models generating all our software takes us out of the frying pan into an AI controlled fire. The diversity has to extend beyond the code to the models and harnesses too. We seem to have done ok with Internet RFCs not splintering too much, so perhaps formal specs can remain singular. Once that's done, it's time to go let hosts mutate and inoculate each other and generally maximise unpredictability at scale!
3 Digital society is going to have to change
To answer my opening question, I don't think better harnesses and models alone will let software engineering catch up, as they just produce mountains of slop code. We need both of the above; formal specifications that let hosts finally be strict about what they receive instead of liberally accepting whatever shows up, while diversity ensures that things that the specs (inevitably) don't capture doesn't break everywhere, everywhere all at once.
The real upheaval here will be to social coding though. Open source communities have run on social contracts of human review and trust built up over decades, and every single one I'm a member of is struggling under matters of AI disclosure and trust.
At least humans aren't out of a job yet though! Somebody still has to decide what our specs contain, as we have done for decades with RFCs. There's also plenty of new computer science research needed! We need to figure out how to debug diversity when no two nodes run the same code, and on how to force simplicity on systems that agents maintain, and ultimately how we settle the blame games when things do go wrong...
(Thanks to Dave Scott, KC Sivaramakrishnan, Thomas Gazagnaire and Sadiq Jaffer for helpful conversations about this post, and to Yaron Minsky for triggering this line of thought with his eBPF observations)

articles.title: Dirac's Theorem at a Dinner Party
articles.body:
Dirac’s Theorem at a Dinner Party
Gabriel Dirac (the famous graph theorist) was the stepson of Paul Dirac (the even more famous physicist). Paul Dirac spent the last years of his career at Florida State University, and my father took his course in General Relativity in the 1970s.
Gabriel formulated an important theorem about Hamiltonian cycles. In this post I want to give a refresher on Hamiltonian cycles, and go over a fun proof of his theorem that involves a hypothetical dinner party.
Over the course of several decades, Dirac’s theorem was improved when mathematicians formulated similar theorems that work with a broader range of graphs. In the following figure, each theorem is more general than the one to its left. Each graph meets its own theorem’s condition, but none of the ones to its left, and its Hamiltonian cycle is blue.
Why am I writing about Dirac’s Theorem? Well, I wanted to write about a simple proof relating to Hamiltonian cycles as prep for my next post, which will be about Barnette’s Conjecture, one of my favorite graph theory conjectures. It got promoted to a theorem in the 6-Oct-2026 Mathocalypse. In my next post I’ll talk more about that.
A Hamiltonian cycle is a walk along the edges of a graph that visits every vertex exactly once and ends up back where it started. A graph that has one is Hamiltonian.
Hamiltonian cycles are related to the Traveling Salesman Problem (e.g. designing delivery routes for Amazon packages). But my personal favorite application is an old-school computer graphics problem: given a triangle mesh, can you render it using a single triangle strip?
Intuitively, it should be easier to find a Hamiltonian cycle in a graph that has lots of edges relative to its vertex count. In a way, that intuition is what Dirac formalized:
If a simple graph has  vertices, and every vertex has at least  neighbors, then the graph has a Hamiltonian cycle.
The following figure shows a random graph with 10 vertices, where every vertex has exactly 5 neighbors, so the theorem guarantees a Hamiltonian cycle. On the right, the same graph has been rearranged so that its Hamiltonian cycle runs around the outside…like a circular dinner table.
1. Dinner party
To see why the theorem is true, first imagine a party where each guest is a vertex and each friendship is an edge. Friendship goes both ways, and nobody is their own friend, which is what simple means in graph theory. A Hamiltonian cycle is a way to seat everyone at a round table so that each guest sits between two friends:
If a party has  guests, and every guest is friends with at least  of the others, then the guests can sit at a round table such that each one sits between two friends.
Here’s the plan. Seat everyone in random order. Two guests who sit side by side are seatmates, and they might be friends, or strangers. Seatmates who are friends get a blue edge, and other friends get a gray edge. Seatmates who are strangers make a gap, which gets a dotted orange line. Here’s the graph from before as a party, seated in random order, with four gaps:
So, if we can find a way that always gets rid of all the gaps, then we will have shown that the theorem is true. We’ll do it with a sequence of moves somewhat akin to playing musical chairs.
2. Musical chairs
Say that strangers  and  sit side by side, with  just clockwise of . And say that somewhere else at the table, there are two more seatmates,  and , with  just clockwise of , where  is a friend of , and  is a friend of .
Here’s the move: everyone from  clockwise around to  stands up, and sits back down in the reverse order. That’s a flip. Afterward,  sits next to , and  sits next to , and those are both pairs of friends.
In the following figure, the stretch that flips is shaded blue. Drag the slider under it to watch it flip.
A flip closes the gap between  and , and opens no new gap.
Why is Lemma 1 true? Inside the stretch that flips, each guest has the same two seatmates as before, just on opposite sides. So the only seatmates who change are at the two endpoints. Before the flip, those were  and , who are strangers, and  and . After the flip, they’re  and , and  and , who are friends. (If  and  were strangers too, then the flip closes two gaps at once.)
The friendship of  and , and the friendship of  and , cross like an X. Let’s call a pair of friendships like that a crossing: one from  to , and one from  to the guest just clockwise of . Each crossing gives a flip.
The following interactive figure runs the algorithm on the party from before, starting with the seating arrangement that happens to have four gaps, and flips until there are none.
Here’s the algorithm:
seat everyone in any order
while some strangers u and v sit side by side, with v just clockwise of u:
    find a friend x of u who sits just counterclockwise of a friend y of v
    reverse the order of everyone from v around to x
So the whole proof comes down to one question. Do gaps always have corresponding crossings? In the next section we’ll answer that question.
3. Pass the potatoes
Recall that  is the number of guests at the party. Let’s write  for the number of friends of guest . Here’s what we seek to prove:
Say strangers  and  sit side by side, with  just clockwise of , and . Then somewhere at the table, a friend of  sits just counterclockwise of a friend of .
One way to see how this is true is the following thought experiment. Give a red potato to each friend of , and a Yukon Gold to each friend of . That’s  potatoes, which is at least . Then everyone with a red potato passes it one seat clockwise, like this:
After that, note that  can no longer hold any potatoes. So the other  guests hold all of the potatoes. Therefore, since there are at least  total potatoes, some guest holds two.
Let’s use  to refer to a guest with two potatoes (circled above). They have a Yukon Gold, so  is a friend of . The red one came from the guest just counterclockwise of , who is a friend of , and that’s . That’s the crossing.
Back to Dirac’s theorem. If every guest has at least  friends, then for any two strangers, , so every gap has a crossing (Lemma 2). Each flip closes a gap and opens none (Lemma 1), so the number of gaps drops with every flip, until there are none, and everyone sits between two friends.
4. References
Edgar Palmer discovered this proof in the work of Øystein Ore and wrote about it in The hidden algorithm of Ore’s theorem on Hamiltonian cycles (though he did not use dinner tables and potatoes).
Dirac’s theorem first appeared in his paper Some theorems on abstract graphs, in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society in 1952.
Homo sapiens. What an inventive, invincible species.
— The Fourth Doctor, The Ark in Space (1975)

Show HN: The Riemann Proof Handbook
articles.body:
A book, in PDF and EPUB, that writes the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis in tamnd/riemann-lean as mathematics: definitions, theorems, lemmas and their proofs, in words.
The claim is not checked. Nobody has built the Lean project in full yet, and no person has checked the written statements against the Lean code. This book explains the Lean code. It is not a separate check of the mathematics. See What is checked.
The books are in the releases.
Each declaration of the proof is inside the dominated subtree of exactly one other declaration (its immediate dominator, in the graph of uses from riemannHypothesis). The ledger gives an entry to each declaration whose dominated subtree is large, in tiers: 1,000 or more declarations (591 entries), 300 or more (1,927), 100 or more (5,764). It assigns each entry to a volume by its branch of the proof or by its Lean folder, and to a chapter by its Lean folder. In a chapter, the entries come from the top of the proof down.
python -m rhb ledger --records /path/to/records --min 1000 --write
ledger/coverage.md has the numbers. prompts/entry.md is the brief for the writers of entries.
You need Python 3.11 or later, pandoc 3.8 or later and Tectonic. Put tamnd/riemann and tamnd/riemann-lean next to this repository.
pip install .
python -m rhb survey
python -m rhb check
python -m rhb build --volume 0,1,2 --formats pdf,epub
The books go to build/. The pipeline is that of The Handbook of Algorithms: Markdown, then pandoc with filters/rhb.lua, then LaTeX with tex/handbook.sty, then Tectonic. The EPUB is EPUB 3 with MathML.
The text is licensed under CC BY 4.0, as the text of tamnd/riemann. The builder is licensed under the MIT licence.
Please report errors at issues.
