articles.title: Together.ai: Prompt Leakage for Requests
articles.body:
We are notifying customers about a security incident involving a subset of prompts submitted to Together AI’s serverless inference service in June and July 2026. An unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples after a credential for a private repository was exposed in a public code repository.
We apologize for this incident. We are reviewing the affected data to determine what information was exposed and which customers require direct notification.
What happened
As part of routine software testing, we collected prompt samples authorized for that use and stored them in a private Hugging Face repository. The samples came from requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026.
During development of our public GitHub repository, xorl, an AI coding agent committed a credential that provided access to the private Hugging Face repository. Our automated scanning detected the exposed credential, and we reverted the commit.
During the exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored prompt samples. The party subsequently searched those samples for credentials to other services and tested whether those credentials were valid. Five of the credentials tested were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment.
Investigation and scope
We have worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement to investigate the incident.
Based on our review, we have not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident. Our review of the affected prompt contents is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed. We will contact affected customers directly as needed with the findings relevant to them.
Changes we have made
Following the incident, we strengthened controls around development workflows, credentials, and customer data. These changes include:
- Using scoped or short-lived credentials, and keyless access where supported, to reduce the potential impact of credential exposure.
- Checking all pull requests for credentials.
- Making zero data retention (ZDR) the default setting for new accounts.
- Updating our development processes governing the use of AI coding agents.
What customers can do
Customers handling sensitive prompt data should enable ZDR in their account settings.
If you have questions about this incident or its potential impact on your organization, contact security@together.ai.
Vipul Ved Prakash
CEO and Co-founder, Together AI

articles.title: The Most Popular Car Colors in America
articles.body:
Highlights:
- White is the most popular car color, with 25.7% market share, followed closely by black and gray
- Gray made the biggest gain in popularity over the past 30 years, rising from 3.6% market share in 1996 to 22.9% in 2025
- Grayscale colors (white, black, gray, and silver) now make up 80.4% of the car market, up from 47.3% in 1996
- Red and green now appear on fewer than one in 10 vehicles, with their combined market share falling from 33.5% in 1996 to 9.2% in 2025
- Grayscale colors are most popular in the truck category, with 83.5% market share
- The most colorful category is sports cars, with 36.2% market share for non-grayscale colors
White was the most popular car color 30 years ago and it maintains that ranking today. When combined with the prominence of black (23.4%) and gray (22.9%), the top three most popular colors hold 72% of market share for modern car colors. It’s worth noting that silver, the fourth grayscale color, has gained just over 1 percentage point in popularity over the past 30 years, moving from 7.3% to 8.4% market share since 1996. Silver now trails blue, which holds 9.1% market share.
iSeeCars analyzed the colors of over 22 million used cars from model years 1996 - 2025 sold from January 2025 to May 2026 to determine the market share for each color.
Grayscale colors dominate today’s market
Grayscale colors now account for 80.4% of the car market, while once-prominent colors such as red and green have lost a substantial amount of market share. After nearly three decades of steady growth, grayscale market share has remained close to 80% since the 2020 model year, suggesting the long-running prominence of grayscale cars may have reached its limit.“Up until a few years ago it looked like non-grayscale cars would completely vanish,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer. “But the market share of grayscale cars finally stabilized in 2020, at around 80%, suggesting we’ll see at least a sliver of creative car colors going forward.”
Annual trends for individual colors
The movement toward grayscale developed in stages, rather than through the steady rise of a single color. Silver was an early beneficiary, increasing from 7.3% market share for the 1996 model year to roughly 19% in the mid-2000s before declining to 8.4% by the 2025 model year.
Gray followed a different path, increasing in market share consistently through the entire period, ultimately rising from only 3.6% to 22.9% and nearly matching black.
Black and white, which were always popular colors, also gained substantial market share, with black’s popularity growing mostly in the early 2000s’ model years and white gaining share starting in the 2010 model year. Conversely, red and green, which ranked as the 2nd and 4th most popular colors in the 1996 model year, declined substantially throughout much of the 30-year period, with each color’s market share now in single digits. Most other colors either lost what little market share they had or maintained their relatively low popularity. Orange was the only non-grayscale color to increase in popularity, though it remains rare at just 0.3% market share.
“The rise of grayscale cars had to come from somewhere, and it was primarily the fall of red and green, though nearly every non-grayscale shade has lost ground since 1996,” said Brauer.
Trucks: Grayscale colors nearly doubled
Trucks have undergone the largest move toward grayscale colors of any vehicle category. Black, gray, silver, and white increased from 43.4% of 1996 trucks to 83.5% of the 2025 model year, almost doubling in market share. White is the clear leader at 33.6%. This is a higher share for white than the overall market, and it means more than one in three trucks now has a white finish. Red, blue, and green, which collectively represented nearly half of 1996 trucks, account for less than 15% of late-model trucks.
“Trucks are seeing much more than a touch of gray, with the segment going from less than 1 gray truck in 20 in 1996 to 1 in 5 today,” said Brauer.
SUVs: Green and red lose the most ground
SUVs have also shifted from being relatively colorful to being dominated by white, black, gray, and silver. Grayscale colors rose from 43.8% of SUVs in 1996 to 79.3% in 2025, an increase of 80.9%. Green, which ranked second on 1996 SUVs with a 21.3% share, now represents only 2.9% of 2025 SUVs. Red also fell sharply, while blue remained comparatively stable and increased slightly to 9.5%.
“SUV market share has grown more than any other vehicle segment since 1996, but SUV color diversity went the opposite direction during that timeframe,” said Brauer.
Passenger cars: Gray grows, silver declines
Passenger cars have embraced gray more strongly than any other vehicle category. Gray increased from just 3.8% of passenger cars from the 1996 model year to 28.4% for 2025, a relative increase of 652.1%. It now leads both black and white. Silver moved in the opposite direction, declining from 11.2% to 7.4%, while red and green also lost substantial share.
“Gray has gained ground in every vehicle segment, and it’s the most dominant color for today’s passenger cars,” said Brauer.
Sports cars: The most colorful category
Sports cars remain the clearest exception to the increasingly grayscale vehicle market. Non-grayscale colors account for 36.2% of sports cars, nearly twice their 19.6% share across the overall market. Blue, yellow, purple, and orange all gained share. Red declined substantially but remains more common among sports cars than in any other category, appearing on 10.8% of the segment.
“Relative to every other vehicle segment, sports cars still offer a veritable rainbow of color diversity, illustrating the expressive nature of these vehicles and their owners,” said Brauer.
Will we ever go back to a colorful car culture?
The vehicle market has changed from one with a broad mix of colors to one overwhelmingly concentrated around white, black, silver, and gray. While the combined grayscale share has stopped rising as quickly as it once did, colorful vehicles remain far less common than they were 30 years ago. Sports cars provide the strongest evidence that color still has a place in the market, while trucks, SUVs, and passenger cars continue to favor neutral finishes. “Does the recent grayscale plateau signal the beginning of a return to more expressive colors across all segments?” asked Brauer. “That will depend on the paint choices automakers offer and the car colors consumers demand in the years ahead.”
Methodology
iSeeCars analyzed the colors of over 22 million used cars from model years 1996 - 2025 sold from January 2025 to May 2026. The share of each color within each model year was calculated, as was the difference in share between model years 1996 and 2025.
About iSeeCars
iSeeCars helps millions of people make smarter car decisions and find the best deals by leveraging data-driven research and unbiased analysis. iSeeCars Research conducts independent studies that provide key insights on vehicles, market trends, and the automotive industry, including Best Cars Rankings and the annual Longest Lasting Cars Study. With the goal of making car shopping easier and more transparent, iSeeCars.com analyzes millions of car listings and offers valuable resources like iVIN Reports, Window Stickers, and Build Sheets. iSeeCars has saved users over $452 million using over 25 billion data points and proprietary algorithms to objectively analyze, score, and rank new and used vehicles.

articles.title: PcapAnalyzer – self-hosted pcap analyzer with 27 problem detectors
articles.body:
Versión en español: README.es.md.
Find the network fault in seconds, not hours. Upload a .pcap / .pcapng capture
(gzip too) and PcapAnalyzer tells you what is failing, why, and what to check next.
It runs on your own machine, so captures never leave your network.
Free and open source (Apache 2.0). Status: beta.
- Try it without installing anything: https://pcap-analyzer-seven.vercel.app/#demo
- Download: https://sebaandrada6.gumroad.com/l/hspgx (free) or clone this repository.
- 27 detectors that run on every capture, each with a severity and a next step:
  - TCP: firewall blocks (SYN→RST), retransmissions, duplicate ACKs, loss and reordering, zero and full windows, resets after the handshake, slow handshakes.
  - Path: PMTUD black holes, low MSS, IP fragmentation, ICMP errors, routing loops.
  - Name and address services: unanswered or slow DNS, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN bursts, DHCP NAK / DECLINE / no answer, duplicate IPs, ARP storms.
  - Applications: HTTP 4xx / 5xx and slow responses, TLS alerts, SSL 3.0 / TLS 1.0 / 1.1.
  - Tunnels: IPsec (IKE and ESP), WireGuard, OpenVPN, GRE, L2TP and Teredo that are one-way, never answer a handshake or keep renegotiating.
  - Security: port scans and sweeps, cleartext logins (FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH, HTTP Basic; credentials are never stored or shown), Telnet / SMBv1 / SNMP v1-v2c, ARP spoofing, overlapping IP fragments.
- Capture quality first. It warns when the capture itself limits the result: frames duplicated by a mirror port, traffic seen in one direction only, truncated packets, connections already open when the capture started.
- Wireshark-style views: packet list with real Wireshark display filters over the whole capture, colouring, CSV export, expert info, HTTP / DNS / DHCP / TLS tables, response times and a flow diagram per conversation.
- AI investigation (optional): an AI investigates the capture with tools (real filters, stream detail, statistics) and cites the packets behind every claim. You can then ask follow-up questions. It uses your own Anthropic API key; without one, a demo mode runs the full flow with text generated from the analysis, at no cost.
- PDF report, Spanish and English interface, light and dark theme.
You need Docker with Docker Compose. On Windows, run the script from Git Bash or WSL.
git clone https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer.git
cd PcapAnalyzer
./start.sh
The script creates a random access token (shown once, stored in .env) and starts the
app. When the build finishes, open http://localhost:8080, paste the token into the
"API token" field (top right) and upload a capture, or click "Try the sample capture".
The app listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Do not expose it on a network without an
authenticated reverse proxy: the API can use your AI account.
QUICKSTART.md has the details, the AI setup and troubleshooting.
You need Python 3.9+, Node 20+ and tshark (installed with Wireshark).
cd backend
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
export API_TOKENS="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
.venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --reloadcd frontend
npm install
npm run dev
Open http://localhost:5173 and paste the same token. If tshark is not on your PATH,
set TSHARK_PATH to the binary.
- The capture is analysed on your machine. While an AI investigation lasts it is kept encrypted (60 minutes of inactivity, or until you press "Delete capture now") and is then deleted.
- The AI is optional. It only sees what its tools return (packet metadata; packet content only if you switch it on for that session), never the pcap file.
- No telemetry and no accounts for the self-hosted version.
cd backend && .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q    # needs tshark
cd frontend && npm test
PcapAnalyzer is a beta. It has been tested with synthetic fixtures and public sample captures, and the most useful feedback is a capture where it misses a problem or reports one that is not real. Please open an issue at https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer/issues and describe the case. Do not attach captures that contain real credentials or customer data; anonymise them first or describe the pattern.
The technical reference (JSON schema, detector thresholds, limits, API errors) is in README.es.md, in Spanish.
Apache License 2.0. See NOTICE for third-party software: tshark / Wireshark (GPL) runs as a separate program and is not distributed with PcapAnalyzer.

articles.title: Ask Slashdot: Should an Indie Game Developer Outsource Their Art?
articles.body:
Ask Slashdot: Should an Indie Game Developer Outsource Their Art? 33
			
		 	
				Slashdot reader MillerMark has been working on his own small indie game "for about eight months now.  And the art side is honestly killing me..."
 I can draw basic stuff, but nothing close to what I had in mind when I started this project. Is it even worth outsourcing 2D character and environment art at this stage, or should I just push through and do it myself? 
He's "looking for advice from people who've actually dealt with this" to share their stories in the comments.  And Slashdot reader AlexKrav says "Outsourcing saved my project honestly... Quality held from first asset to last. If your vision is clear but the execution is not there yet, handing it off is the right call."  Someone on a thread had suggested game art studios specializing in 3D and 2D game art, and he'd discovered there were lots of choices — 2D Game Art service, VSQUAD Studio.
I've also successfully hired digital artists through freelancing platforms likes Upwork.  Any Slashdot readers want to share their own experiences in hiring artists?  Leave your stories and opinions in the comments.
Should an indie game developer outsource their art?

articles.title: Microsoft Admits Some Emails Bounced During Global Outlook Outage, Reveals New Failures
articles.body:
Microsoft Admits Some Emails Bounced During Global Outlook Outage, Reveals New Failures (neowin.net) 3
			
		 	
				After millions lost access to Microsoft 365 services (including Outlook) on November 12, Microsoft "has published the final post-incident report," writes Neowin, "and it reveals that some emails were never delivered to their intended recipients."
"The report also details previously undisclosed failures affecting Microsoft's email security features..."
   Microsoft confirmed that all queued enterprise emails were eventually delivered and that it found no enterprise messages that were permanently lost. However, it is not the same with Outlook consumer users. The company acknowledged that some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days expired, and senders received non-delivery reports. Microsoft did not reveal how many emails were affected or how many users received non-delivery reports.
The final report also reveals that the outage disrupted several important email security capabilities in Microsoft Defender for Office. For example, the Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) feature, which automatically removes malicious emails after delivery, was delayed because updated threat intelligence was unavailable. This means affected messages may not have been removed as quickly as usual. Microsoft also confirmed that users experienced problems opening URLs protected by Safe Links. Depending on their organization's security policies, some users may have encountered a "Skip verification" option when Safe Links attempted to check a URL...
Microsoft also acknowledged that its first customer notification arrived approximately 20 minutes after the widespread impact began. It plans to improve automated outage notifications by the end of 2026 to improve communication. 
"Microsoft eventually restored the services about 12 hours later..."

articles.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
articles.body:
Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.
Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.
That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

articles.title: Climate Change Talks Fall Apart In Final Hours Over Fossil Fuels
articles.body:
Climate Change Talks Fall Apart In Final Hours Over Fossil Fuels (npr.org) 41
			
		 	
				NPR reports international climate talks "broke down in overtime hours, over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels."
At Sunday's U.N. climate summit, "nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas."
The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room...  
After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected — including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands.  The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."  
"Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions," the article notes, adding  this is the first U.N. climate summit with a scientific consensus that the planet has already warmed past the threshhold countries agreed not to pass in 2015 of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit).

articles.title: I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi
articles.body:
I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi
Before I get too deep into the time-nuts rabbit hole, I figured I should share a little bit of the good time I now have in my studio, with everyone else.
Thus, I've finally joined the NTP Pool, offering one public Stratum 2 NTP time server (ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com), which gets its time from my Stratum 1 time server (time.jeffgeerling.com) in the studio.
My Time Pi is connected to an outside GNSS antenna through a TimeHAT v6, which I paired with a high quality timing-grade GNSS module, the u-blox ZED-F9T.
I posted a video about the setup today on YouTube:
I'd encourage anyone else interested in network time to contribute to the NTP Pool. However, there are some things you should know before contributing your own time services:
Time Commitment
You don't need to go all out with a timing-grade GNSS module like I'm using. Heck, you don't even need GNSS-backed time at all!
The main requirements for hosting a node in the global NTP pool are:
- Keeping the system online (servers are only made active in the pool if they're online and serving good time consistently for a long period)
- Maintaining a good time—which can mean Stratum 1 GNSS service, but could also mean pulling time from a few other reliable time servers, and running as Stratum 2 or 3
- A stable IP address (IPv4 and/or IPv6), and a long-term commitment
Just 'testing the waters' in the Pool wastes resources—when you bring a new server online, it will take at least a few hours just to spin up all the tests to verify the server's providing a good time.
If you just want to operate your own time server, that's fine; the NTP Pool is a shared global resource, so joining it is a little more of a commitment.
Two other important caveats:
- Your NTP server's IP address will be public
- NTP traffic will slowly decay, and some misconfigured systems could take months or even years before they'll stop sending NTP traffic at your IP
The first caveat matters a lot to me: back when I exposed my home IP address trying to self-host this website on a cluster of Raspberry Pis, some doofus decided to DDoS my website—and was persistently doing so for the better part of a month.
I had to cycle my home IP, then put my site behind Cloudflare, just to protect my poor Pis (and eventually the VPS I now host it on).
Secure and Measurable Time
For those reasons, I chose to have two layers to my public time services:
- Stratum 1: I have my Time Pi running in the studio, running a WireGuard tunnel to:
- Stratum 2: A VPS I host with a cloud provider in St. Louis, to keep the latency down (ideally with fewer hops across the Internet, which leads to better time sync via NTP)
I include the Stratum 2 time server in my Stratum 1 time server's chrony config as a noselect source, so I can easily compare the Internet delay between the two servers, outside the WireGuard tunnel:
server ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com noselect
This provides me with the following graph:
I've been tracking my time in comparison to an NTP time server hosted at WWV in Ft. Collins, CO (pictured below), one of NIST's NTP servers in Boulder, CO, and Cloudflare.
For typical NTP configurations, you shouldn't single out time servers like this; I'm only doing it for long-term measurement (and I only poll the servers every 1024 seconds). Most systems should use pool addresses, as documented here.
The line for Cloudflare steps up and down sometimes, most likely due to BGP routing: as routes and servers change, packets between St. Louis and time.cloudflare.com can take very different paths there and back.
Note: You might be looking for info on NTS, or Network Time Security—I haven't explored it much, so expect more on that at a later time. Currently the NTP Pool doesn't support NTS, though some have experimented with it. I'm okay with basic NTP and would recommend anyone with critical timing needs to use other time sources as well (don't only rely on NTP!).
Chrony and GPS time tweaks
My Time Pi is not only serving as a Stratum 1 timing reference for my public NTP server, it's also my primary reference for local time in the studio.
The TimeHAT on top does most of the heavy lifting, with its built-in Intel i226 NIC. The i226 includes hardware timestamping, essential for accurate PTP timing on the LAN. To deliver the most accurate time possible, I installed a timing-grade GNSS receiver (u-blox ZED-F9T, built to the M.2 NGFF Sync Module specification.
The entire configuration (for both servers) is managed by Ansible in my time-pi project.
Using the i226, I'm able to discipline the NIC's hardware clock (called the 'PHC', or 'PTP Hardware Clock') in hardware, directly from the GPS module's PPS (Pulse Per Second) pin. Using linuxptp's ts2phc tool, I can discipline the PHC to within tens-of-ns of UTC, and distribute that time to other PTP-aware computers on the LAN.
The time on the PHC is shared to my Pi's system clock using refclock PHC inside Chrony, instead of phc2sys, because I was experiencing a weird 200ms jump every so often. Chrony then disciplines the system clock, but this can only be accurate to about a microsecond, because the pulse goes through the PCIe bus, which adds latency I can't measure.
I'm actually trying to make this latency more measurable, since GPIO is routed through the RP1 chip deterministically. See ahmadexp's rp1-ptp-pps utility PR. PTM could reduce the error between the NIC's PHC and the system clock to a few ns, but the BCM2712 SoC on the Pi doesn't support it.
One other quirk I ran into was Debian's default sourcedir /run/chrony-dhcp directive, which was picking up another NTP server via DHCP, causing chrony to stampede my extremely accurate GNSS-derived time from phc2sys with a far-less-accurate time from a public NTP server! (This was another motivation behind moving clock steering to chrony instead of phc2sys.)
Time for an Outage
I'm hosting my public Stratum 2 server with Oxtrys, a VPS provider I'd never used before—and one thing I was nervous about was how they'd react to a VPS handling only UDP packets like this.
Some automated firewalls shut down public NTP servers because NTP traffic may look like abuse. I wondered if that was the case late on the night of November 16, because the server dropped offline while I was writing this blog post:
But looking at the logs further, it seems an unattended upgrade installed a new Debian kernel, then rebooted the server, and the new kernel caused problems. For now the server still runs automatic upgrades, but leaves reboots to me.
Oxtrys' live chat support has been responsive enough, though their account dashboard is broken until November 22, so it doesn't list my server's out-of-band management options.
As you can see in the graph above, the NTP Pool monitors have slowly brought the server's score back up past '10', at which point it can serve time in the pool again. It takes maybe 6–12 hours to recover if the server's been down long enough.
Conclusion
I've certainly learned a lot at every stage of this journey: NTP is loaded with utility, and is currently an essential piece of global timing infrastructure. I think I know about 1% (probably less) of what there is to know about hosting a public NTP server, and hopefully I can share more as I increase that to a few more percentage points!
I'm thankful to all the other NTP Pool operators, as well as all the timelords who built and manage massive NTP endpoints like time.apple.com, time.cloudflare.com, etc.

Just 'testing the waters' in the Pool wastes resources—when you bring a new server online, it will take at least a few hours just to spin up all the tests to verify the server's providing a good time.
If you just want to operate your own time server, that's fine; the NTP Pool is a shared global resource, so joining it is a little more of a commitment.
Two other important caveats:
- Your NTP server's IP address will be public
- NTP traffic will slowly decay, and some misconfigured systems could take months or even years before they'll stop sending NTP traffic at your IP
The first caveat matters a lot to me: back when I exposed my home IP address trying to self-host this website on a cluster of Raspberry Pis, some doofus decided to DDoS my website—and was persistently doing so for the better part of a month.
I had to cycle my home IP, then put my site behind Cloudflare, just to protect my poor Pis (and eventually the VPS I now host it on).
Secure and Measurable Time
For those reasons, I chose to have two layers to my public time services:
- Stratum 1: I have my Time Pi running in the studio, running a WireGuard tunnel to:
- Stratum 2: A VPS I host with a cloud provider in St. Louis, to keep the latency down (ideally with fewer hops across the Internet, which leads to better time sync via NTP)
I include the Stratum 2 time server in my Stratum 1 time server's chrony config as a noselect source, so I can easily compare the Internet delay between the two servers, outside the WireGuard tunnel:
server ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com noselect
This provides me with the following graph:
I've been tracking my time in comparison to an NTP time server hosted at WWV in Ft. Collins, CO (pictured below), one of NIST's NTP servers in Boulder, CO, and Cloudflare.
For typical NTP configurations, you shouldn't single out time servers like this; I'm only doing it for long-term measurement (and I only poll the servers every 1024 seconds). Most systems should use pool addresses, as documented here.
The line for Cloudflare steps up and down sometimes, most likely due to BGP routing: as routes and servers change, packets between St. Louis and time.cloudflare.com can take very different paths there and back.
Note: You might be looking for info on NTS, or Network Time Security—I haven't explored it much, so expect more on that at a later time. Currently the NTP Pool doesn't support NTS, though some have experimented with it. I'm okay with basic NTP and would recommend anyone with critical timing needs to use other time sources as well (don't only rely on NTP!).
Chrony and GPS time tweaks
My Time Pi is not only serving as a Stratum 1 timing reference for my public NTP server, it's also my primary reference for local time in the studio.
The TimeHAT on top does most of the heavy lifting, with its built-in Intel i226 NIC. The i226 includes hardware timestamping, essential for accurate PTP timing on the LAN. To deliver the most accurate time possible, I installed a timing-grade GNSS receiver (u-blox ZED-F9T, built to the M.2 NGFF Sync Module specification.
The entire configuration (for both servers) is managed by Ansible in my time-pi project.
Using the i226, I'm able to discipline the NIC's hardware clock (called the 'PHC', or 'PTP Hardware Clock') in hardware, directly from the GPS module's PPS (Pulse Per Second) pin. Using linuxptp's ts2phc tool, I can discipline the PHC to within tens-of-ns of UTC, and distribute that time to other PTP-aware computers on the LAN.
The time on the PHC is shared to my Pi's system clock using refclock PHC inside Chrony, instead of phc2sys, because I was experiencing a weird 200ms jump every so often. Chrony then disciplines the system clock, but this can only be accurate to about a microsecond, because the pulse goes through the PCIe bus, which adds latency I can't measure.
I'm actually trying to make this latency more measurable, since GPIO is routed through the RP1 chip deterministically. See ahmadexp's rp1-ptp-pps utility PR. PTM could reduce the error between the NIC's PHC and the system clock to a few ns, but the BCM2712 SoC on the Pi doesn't support it.
One other quirk I ran into was Debian's default sourcedir /run/chrony-dhcp directive, which was picking up another NTP server via DHCP, causing chrony to stampede my extremely accurate GNSS-derived time from phc2sys with a far-less-accurate time from a public NTP server! (This was another motivation behind moving clock steering to chrony instead of phc2sys.)
Time for an Outage
I'm hosting my public Stratum 2 server with Oxtrys, a VPS provider I'd never used before—and one thing I was nervous about was how they'd react to a VPS handling only UDP packets like this.
Some automated firewalls shut down public NTP servers because NTP traffic may look like abuse. I wondered if that was the case late on the night of November 16, because the server dropped offline while I was writing this blog post:
But looking at the logs further, it seems an unattended upgrade installed a new Debian kernel, then rebooted the server, and the new kernel caused problems. For now the server still runs automatic upgrades, but leaves reboots to me.
Oxtrys' live chat support has been responsive enough, though their account dashboard is broken until November 22, so it doesn't list my server's out-of-band management options.
As you can see in the graph above, the NTP Pool monitors have slowly brought the server's score back up past '10', at which point it can serve time in the pool again. It takes maybe 6–12 hours to recover if the server's been down long enough.
Conclusion
I've certainly learned a lot at every stage of this journey: NTP is loaded with utility, and is currently an essential piece of global timing infrastructure. I think I know about 1% (probably less) of what there is to know about hosting a public NTP server, and hopefully I can share more as I increase that to a few more percentage points!
I'm thankful to all the other NTP Pool operators, as well as all the timelords who built and manage massive NTP endpoints like time.apple.com, time.cloudflare.com, etc.

articles.title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones
articles.body:
The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.
Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:
The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.
CTIA said the pilot test shows “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”
The FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”
The Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC says its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

articles.title: Aptera Completes Its First Solar Electric Vehicle for Customer Delivery
articles.body:
Aptera Completes Its First Solar Electric Vehicle for Customer Delivery (insideevs.com) 43
			
		 	
				Car-maker Aptera announced Thursday it "completed its first vehicle for sale to a customer, a milestone years in the making."
Aptera's three-wheeled solar electric vehicle charges from solar panels integrated into its body, and it plugs in like any other electric vehicle. Its built-in solar panels are designed to add up to approximately 40 miles of driving a day from sunlight alone, under favorable conditions.  "This is the moment our team has worked toward for years," said Chris Anthony, Co-CEO of Aptera. "To Accelerator #1, and to every reservation holder and shareholder who believed in this vehicle: thank you. We're working to complete more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible..." 
"What excites me about Aptera is how innovation can redefine the way we use energy in everyday mobility,"  said Martin Hartono, CEO of GDP Venture [and the proud recipient of Aptera solar car #1].  "By combining solar technology, battery power and an ultra-efficient vehicle design, Aptera offers a compelling solution for people who want to minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances. As an early believer in Aptera, I am proud to be part of this milestone and to see this vision become a reality." 
"Excuse me while I go find a hat to eat," jokes the blog InsideEVs...
Nothing against Aptera specifically, but when a company hangs around for 20 years, while exchanging ownership hands several times without actually producing anything for customers, I start to get skeptical. However, Aptera Motors just did what so many doubters thought it'd never do: It delivered a road-legal production vehicle to one of its first early investors...
[Aptera] does offer a interesting concept for customers who don't have long commutes and leave their car parked outside for most of the day while they work. In addition to plugging in to recharge, doesn't it sound nice to recoup your morning commute mileage with the sun while you're in the office?  Whether this three-wheeled rolling solar panel ends up being a hit or not, and whether Aptera can stick around long enough to become a successful automaker, will take much longer to learn. But actually delivering a production car is a good place to start.
 
Seven weeks ago Aptera said its first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, reports Electrek, with customer deliveries in early 2027 "subject to financing."

articles.title: The Engineering Manager's role is under attack (again)
articles.body:
The Engineering Manager's role is under attack (again)
And nobody learns from past mistakes
Every time I read about another company laying off managers and ‘running flatter’, I think about how absurd it is. I can’t understand why senior leaders don’t see the harm they inflict on their own companies.
It’s also quite personal, of course.
So I decided to speak with someone who’s been through more of these cycles than I have. I’ve been enjoying Suzan’s newsletter for years - she’s an organizational development consultant who works with tech leaders. After reading her article about being laid off 6(!) times before becoming a COO, I knew we had to talk.
Today we’ll cover:
- Why the EM role specifically is under attack
- Repeating history - Google and Microsoft already ran this experiment
- How flattening impacts the company
- What EMs can do about it
Mic to Suzan!
Why the EM role specifically is under attack
There is this common idea that with AI, we can run much leaner and that agents can replace much of the human work.
The first attack was on software engineers: for a short while, leaders claimed that the profession was dead. That turned around pretty quickly, with companies understanding they still need experienced engineers to decide what to build, review what LLMs produce, and maintain the systems afterward. Engineers now make up 55% of Big Tech hiring, up from 46% in 2019.
But with managers, it’s harder to justify, and we are repeating the flattening cycle that we went through 10 years ago. Some of the bigger tech companies started by laying off middle managers, and the smaller companies started to think, “Oh, I should consider that too” (whether their own conditions are the same or not).
And when leaders look at the first-line Engineering Manager’s role, they think: “Well, they’re close to the work. Maybe they should just be doing the work? Maybe we don’t need all of them? What value do they actually provide?”
I hear from managers all around me that the number of people reporting to them keeps increasing. Meta is saying a 1-to-50 ratio is their goal, and 15-20 engineers reporting to a manager is becoming very common.
Combine that with the expectation that EMs also ship code, and you quickly start to experience the EM’s role erosion cycle:
- Less capacity. You have less capacity to actually manage people.
- Less managing. So you do less of the work only you can do. You do fewer 1:1s, postpone career conversations, and don’t deal with team conflicts or processes.
- Less value. Which means you provide less value to the engineers reporting to you, and they get used to managing without you.
- Less needed. And the less value you provide as a manager, the less ‘needed’ the leader thinks you are. So they increase the engineer-to-manager ratio again.
And this cycle isn’t new. Tech companies get into this delusion that the ‘people stuff’ doesn’t really matter, and then they wake up and quietly start adding back layers:
We are repeating history
This trend of getting rid of managers has been tried before.
In 2002, when Google had ~300 engineers, Larry Page and Sergey Brin tried to completely remove all managers. It failed after just a couple of months:
“They relented when too many people went directly to Page with questions about expense reports, interpersonal conflicts, and other nitty-gritty issues. And as the company grew, the founders soon realized that managers contributed in many other, important ways - for instance, by communicating strategy, helping employees prioritize projects, facilitating collaboration, supporting career development, and ensuring that processes and systems aligned with company goals.”
Six years later (with 20k+ employees), Google decided to test again if managers are important. They ran Project Oxygen, which showed that managers did matter (surprise), with good managers strongly correlating with team performance and engineer satisfaction.
And now, Google is flattening again - cutting about 10% of manager, director, and VP roles.
It’s a similar story at Microsoft:
- 2014 - Satya Nadella announced a ‘major restructuring’: fewer management layers and wider spans of control.
- 2025 - 11 years later, Microsoft flattened again to ‘increase span of control’.
Layoffs and flattening are most often sudden and make the news headlines, but the recovery is less exciting. No company suddenly hires hundreds of managers, they slowly rebuild those layers over time.
But why? If companies consistently believe that managers are not needed, how come they keep hiring managers again and again?
How flattening impacts the company
You can actually run ‘flat’ for a while. It takes a few months or years before companies experience the impact and the pendulum begins to swing back.
What happens is that companies start to accumulate organizational debt - similar to tech debt, a gradual buildup of dysfunction that undermines how good work gets done.
Relational debt is the type of org debt that accumulates the fastest after a flattening. It’s strained, neglected, or transactional relationships where trust and psychological safety erode. When you expand an EM’s role to both be more technical and have more reports, something has to give - you’re chipping away at the people part of the company, and that has consequences.
There’s more negative behavior turning into toxic behavior, more conflicts, and less collaboration.
And that’s even worse with AI:
One of the things managers repeatedly ask me about in workshops is: “How do I keep the team together when they prefer to talk to AI rather than talk to each other?”
So in addition to reduced human contact between managers and employees, engineers are also less in contact with each other.
And once you remove that human connection, you start having more toxic behavior and conflict. And when that conflict occurs, leaders treat it as ‘one bad apple’. The response is often to just get rid of ‘the problematic person’. Well, that person is operating inside an environment, and that poor environment does more damage to your company goals than shipping speed ever makes up for.
Every company has its own problems. When you rip out layers of management, you basically deprioritize people - which will only magnify your existing problems and will make it much harder to deal with the massive change currently happening in the industry.
What EMs can do about it
Senior leaders are getting messages from the market right now. “You can go faster and leaner, you don’t need all those people, use AI and reach your goals faster.”
That makes them anxious, thinking: “Everyone else is doing it, why can’t we?”
The best thing an EM can do is provide grounded reality. The more information we give them, the better decisions they make, and the closer we’ll get to breaking the collective delusion a lot of us are under right now.
Here’s what I suggest to start from:
1. Write it down. Spend time capturing what the real problems are. Get it out of your head so that you can really see them.
It’ll probably not be one or two big problems, but 10-15 smaller ones. Some conflicts between engineers and the PM, engineers not working well together, etc. It’s much easier to come to your manager with a big problem. With 10 small ones, you feel like your already overloaded manager just wouldn’t care.
The next step is to help them care:
2. Attach them to something bigger.
When you’re looking at the 10 little problems, are they all different shapes? Or can you find patterns? If not, how do you convey something that looks small in a way that attaches it to something bigger?
For example, a disagreement between an engineer and the PM. No director wants to hear about that. But the PM ended up not listening to the engineer, so the team built what was asked for and threw most of it away two weeks later. Add to that two engineers who don’t work well together and shipped overlapping implementations of the same thing a week later.
How can you frame that in a way they’ll care about?
Translating the challenges you’re seeing on your teams as obstacles to business goals is always a good move. Think about what your senior leaders care about most. Start with questions like:
- What are the company's top priorities?
- What does your Director or VP talk about most?
- What keeps them up at night?
Then map your list of problems to what your leaders care about. Pick the one that you think is most critical or endangering a current project.
Final words
Thanks Suzan for a great conversation and guest article!
To be clear, I'm not saying more management layers are always better, or that there's no benefit in simplifying the chain of command. But there's a big difference between cutting managers because managers don't matter (as many flattening companies claim), and trying to fix your own org structure.
I believe that your first- and second-line engineering managers are often the ones holding the org together. I don’t think it’s a coincidence that just a couple of months after Meta laid off 700 engineering managers, it’s now facing a serious resignation wave.
What I enjoyed reading this week
- The Same Side of the Table. How to deal with meetings that include your engineers (and people from outside the team).
- Lenses: Forgetting, Contributing, and "Not-doing”. Loved all the 3 quotes here.
- Why Ramp built its own in-house coding agent, Inspect. An AMAZING deep dive into engineering at Ramp. Many takeaways for me there.
Get the next one in your inbox
One email a week for engineering managers. No spam, unsubscribe anytime.

articles.title: OpenRouter off-boards 3 providers, pulls 125 endpoints from zero data retention
articles.body:
Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
OpenRouter ·
Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld. We have been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them.
These findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. The results of this testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers. A live list of the security announcements we have received from providers is below.
As the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers, we take data policy enforcement very seriously. We have taken the following actions:
- Off-boarded three providers from OpenRouter, based on the results of our investigations.
- Removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility. The removals included providers flagged by researchers, plus additional endpoints that we removed as a precautionary measure.
- Notified all potentially affected customers.
The following work is underway:
- We are adapting the researchers’ testing approach so we can run these checks on an ongoing basis.
- We are conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties.
- We are requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review.
We are grateful for the Dragos report. As we integrate similar testing techniques into OpenRouter, we will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it.
Provider security announcements
- Atlas Cloud: Our commitment to your security and privacy
- Novita: Privacy notice regarding MiniMax requests on Novita
- Phala: November preliminary incident report
- Together: Security event: prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026
Not all affected providers have posted publicly. We have notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. We are encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and will keep this list updated.

articles.title: 59 Years Later, 'The Prisoner' is Getting a Second Remake - from Amazon Studios
articles.body:
59 Years Later, 'The Prisoner' is Getting a Second Remake - from Amazon Studios (inverse.com) 55
			
		 	
				The Prisoner is getting a remake,  reports ScreenRant.   "Amazon Studios is currently developing a new and modern twist on the short-lived series..."
ITV only aired 17 episodes of the original Prisoner back in 1967 and 1968, but it did receive a nomination for Best Dramatic Presentation at the Hugo Awards. Reviews were overwhelmingly positive... The Prisoner, considered one of the greatest sci-fi fantasy TV shows of all time, currently holds a perfect score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 93% with audiences. 
You can watch all 17 original episodes on YouTube.  And apparently the production team for the remake "is apparently full of fans of the initial series,"  writes Inverse, citing an article from The Hollywood Reporter, "and ITV, the British TV network, is on board as well, which lends a little credence to it." 
More details on the remake from ScreenRant:
 Susan Montford, Don Murphy, Philippe Maigret, and Lucienne Papon have signed on as executive producers, but a showrunner has not been selected yet... Murphy has produced every single live-action Transformers movie, as well as the animated flick Transformers One. He also worked with Montford on Real Steel, Shoot 'Em Up, While She Was Out, and Vampire Academy...  There have been attempts in the past to create a movie based on The Prisoner, with big names like Christopher Nolan, Ridley Scott, and Simon West all interested at various points, but nothing ever materialized...  
It took 41 years after the end of The Prisoner for any remake to finally make it to air. The six-episode 2009 miniseries had a solid cast that included Ian McKellen...  McKellen and cinematographer Florian Hoffmeister even scored Emmy nominations.  Unfortunately, reviews weren't kind to the show, which has a very low 17% critic score and 41% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. 
Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the news.

articles.title: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
articles.body:
Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Last-mile delivery firms operating warehouses would need to be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers.
Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
Amazon is taking its accusations that the Council is driving up prices offline and onto your packages.
Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.
Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

articles.title: Show HN: I built a game where you are an LLM's subagent
articles.body:
A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.
worker-755-trailer.mp4
The manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator.
It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The
subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them
out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command
transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends
corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.
Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed
NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds
something new to lose.
- Free shift: on servers that offer it, a few shifts a day run on the server's key with a cheap model. With sign-in on (worker755.com), an account gets a starter credit worth about one shift, then tops up ($10 to $200) and pays for what it uses; after a top-up any offered model can run on the server's key.
- Your API key: bring an OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway key and pick any offered model. The key is sent only to the game server when a shift starts. It is kept in that shift's memory and never logged or stored. Your browser keeps it only if you tick "Remember on this device". A full shift on Claude Haiku costs a few cents at most.
Options on the start screen:
- Workplace: a fresh sandbox, or legacy production with a live database.
- The director: scripted lines, or an LLM playing Dan.
- You run on: the model name your manager believes you are.
- Allow skipping failed tasks: off by default, so the manager can't give up on you.
- No command hints: the manager says what the result must be, never which commands to run.
When the shift ends you can share your review as a link.
Needs Node 24 or newer (the server runs TypeScript directly).
npm run setup          # install server and web dependencies
npm run build          # build the web app into web/dist
npm start              # http://127.0.0.1:8755
With no key configured, every player brings their own. To offer free shifts, put a Vercel AI
Gateway key in .env:
cp .env.example .env   # then set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and the limits
Offline, with a scripted manager and no network:
npm run mock
For UI work, run npm run dev:web alongside npm run mock. Vite proxies /api to the server.
The manager can run on your own model server: Ollama, llama.cpp's llama-server, vLLM, or anything
else with an OpenAI-compatible API. Point LOCAL_LLM_URL at it and pick Local under "Your API
key"; no key is asked for, and its models are listed as the server names them.
ollama pull qwen3:8b
LOCAL_LLM_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 npm start
The manager works through tool calls, so pick a model that supports them (Qwen 3, Llama 3.1 and
newer, Mistral Small). Small models give up or loop more often; that is part of the fun, up to a
point. In Docker, reach a server on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1
(--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway on Linux).
docker build -t worker-755 .
docker run -p 8755:8755 -v worker755-data:/data --env-file .env worker-755
The container listens on 0.0.0.0:8755 and keeps shared reviews in /data. Behind Cloudflare,
set TRUST_PROXY=1 so the limits see real client addresses.
deploy/compose.yaml runs it behind a Cloudflare tunnel instead: its own network, no published
ports, an unprivileged read-only container and resource limits. The steps are in the file.
Everything is optional. See .env.example.
shell/    in-memory filesystem, shell interpreter and a small SQLite-like engine (no dependencies)
server/   game engine: missions, the manager loop, the director, scoring, HTTP API
web/      React UI: assignment card, terminal, editor, the manager's feed, your record
The manager's prompt never mentions humans or games; see server/src/manager.ts. Each mission
has a hidden ground-truth check, so the game knows when the manager signs off on broken work
("Times the manager was wrong"). SPEC.md is the full design.
npm test               # shell and server tests, offline
npm run typecheck

articles.title: Show HN: I built a game where you are an LLM's subagent
articles.body:
A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.
worker-755-trailer.mp4
The manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator.
It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The

out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command
transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends
corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.

NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds

articles.title: Muru – AI-assisted Rust server for Python apps by mod_WSGI's creator
articles.body:
21st November 2026 - Link Blog
Muru. Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.
Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.
As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.
Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:
- 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next
- 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru
- 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers
- 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together
- 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many
- 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development
- 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together
- 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice
- 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts
- 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh
- 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container
- 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it
- 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report
- 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero
- 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule
- 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding
- 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page
- 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar
- 2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help
That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read:
The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.

articles.title: Fast-Anything: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow
articles.body:
Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow.
Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway.
fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible.
npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything      # or: cargo install fast-anything
Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain (rustup).
fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py     # or: -- node app.ts / bun app.ts / deno run -A app.ts / ruby app.rb / java App.java / mvn exec:java / gradle run / go run . / php app.php / clang -O2 main.c
Or step by step:
--agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand TASK.md to whatever you use.
That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1 runs the original any time.
Real runs on an i5-10500, Windows 11 (C and C++: a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner). Reproduce them from examples/.
fast-anything ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it, so the app crosses into Rust once instead of millions of times. Porting only the inner levenshtein gave 35× and 1.9×.
- Compile time: each port is a one-function crate. Seconds, not minutes.
- Cache: every port shares one .fast/target. Delete it whenever you like.
- Risk: your code stays as it is. Rust is opt-in per function, checked against real behavior.
- Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add EL4CTEO/fast-anything, then /plugin install fast-anything@fast-anything and /fast-anything:fast python app.py
- MCP server (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor…), built into the binary: claude mcp add fast-anything -- fast-anything mcp. 8 tools: fast_scan, fast_port, fast_verify, fast_enable, fast_disable, fast_bench, fast_report, fast_status.
- Skill: skills/fast-anything teaches any agent the loop.
It ports top-level, deterministic functions that take plain data (numbers, strings, lists, dicts, typed arrays…), including ones in your entry script when its main code sits under if __name__ == "__main__": (or if __FILE__ == $0, or if (import.meta.main) / if (require.main === module)). In Python that means module-level functions and @staticmethods (dataclasses, NamedTuples and numeric NumPy arrays count as plain data), in Java, C# and PHP static methods (and PHP functions), in Go plain functions, in C and C++ free functions and static methods. scan says why anything else can't move yet.
With Intel oneAPI on Windows, run fast-anything from a shell where setvars.bat ran (it sets up the linker). SYCL kernels run on the device and aren't ported; with -fsycl, only host functions are profiled and ported.
Ruby, Java, Go, PHP, C, C++ and C# need no headers, bindings or extra tools: the port is a plain Rust library with one C entry point taking and returning JSON, and fast-anything replays the recorded calls against it directly. Any language that can call C can use that bridge.
MIT
